What Liberians deserve now, at minimum, is a clear public accounting from the administration of what changed between the version Boakai rejected and the version he signed — specifically, what safeguards, if any, will exist by 2028 to keep four independent ports from being four times as vulnerable as the single system that just spent a summer failing to catch a ship sitting in plain view off its own coast. The 18-month transition period is, in effect, the administration’s own self-imposed deadline for answering that question. Until it does, the safest assumption is the least reassuring one: that the law changed, and the vulnerability it was meant to address is being left for 2028 to sort out.

World.title: How a Liberia “Cartel” Took a 71-Year-old Canadian $100k
World.content:
A Canadian retiree’s search for African gold turned into a months-long con involving fake shipping companies, a phony “minister,” strongbox theater, and a scheme so elaborate he compares it to “an academy award performance.”

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – Gerry Pettle wants one thing understood before anything else: he isn’t writing to embarrass himself.



“I am writing you on the advice of two friends of your country,” the 71-year-old Canadian says in a note to FrontPageAfrica explaining why he’s going public, “and not necessarily in agreement to make this complaint a public humiliation of myself.” He calls himself “a Canadian, born young fellow at the age of 71” — a wry touch from a man who, by his own account, was taken for more than $100,000 USD by a network of scammers in Liberia over the course of several months this year.

It started, as these things often do, with a friend of a friend.



A Favor from Sam



Pettle knew a man named Sam Berkel, who in turn knew a man named Paul — a Liberian expatriate originally from Toronto. Paul, Sam said, had a way to get gold out of Liberia. Pettle now calls it what it was: “a scheme.” At the time, he had no reason to doubt it.



Paul asked Pettle and Sam for $20,000 to secure a shipment of gold he’d bring back to Toronto himself. The two split the cost and wired the money in installments — a few thousand dollars a day, spread out to avoid suspicion. The gold never arrived. Paul never flew back. When Pettle finally reached him, the excuses began: a delay, then another delay, then the claim that Paul himself had been robbed — the gold and the money “switched” out from under him by unnamed thieves.



It should have ended there. It didn’t.



The Dubai Pitch



A week later, Paul had a new plan: he’d have a kilo of gold worked into jewelry and meet Pettle in Dubai, where Pettle could collect it, pay off the man Paul supposedly owed, and recoup his original $20,000 plus a profit. The cost of entry this time was smaller — $3,500 for airfare and jewelry-making — but the outcome was the same. The money vanished. So, for a while, did Paul.



When Paul resurfaced, he offered something even more improbable: a stranger claiming to have millions in marked American cash that needed “washing” for a fee. Pettle refused outright. “Paul, F off,” he recalls telling him. “You’re mental.”



Two days later, Paul was back on the phone with yet another connection — a man with a diplomatic passport, capable of moving gold across borders without permits. Paul said he didn’t trust the man directly but knew someone who did: a fixer who went by “Boylan,” whose real name, Pettle later learned, was Jensen Gonkarnue.



Boylan, Peter, and the Compound



Jensen — “Boylan” — called Pettle personally, addressing him warmly as “Doc.” He vouched for a Liberian gold trader named Peter John, describing a house near the residence of Liberia’s president as proof of legitimacy. On a call, Peter told Pettle he had hundreds of kilos of gold sourced from local miners and sent a photograph appearing to show roughly a thousand kilos stacked on a floor. All Pettle had to do, Peter said, was cover the shipping tax.



It was the first of many taxes.



Pettle sent $12,500 by USDT for the initial tax. Then came a $14,500 charge for air freight and insurance to a company calling itself Noble Shipping — complete with an invoice and a bank routing number, giving Pettle, for the first time, something resembling a paper trail. He and a new partner, Robert, paid it. The package, he was told, was on its way.



It was around this time a second trader, a man named Ben, contacted Pettle claiming to have five kilos of his own gold and to have heard of Pettle’s reputation through a woman named Bernice. A pattern was forming — taxes, shipping fees, insurance, one new stranger after another — but Pettle, already deep in, kept going.

Flying to Liberia



By the time Pettle boarded a flight to Liberia in June, he had lost thousands and gained nothing but promises. He was met at the airport by Boylan, carrying a single assayed kilo of gold as “collateral” against the money already spent.



The next day brought a scene Pettle still describes in almost cinematic terms: a drive down a rough, barely marked road to a barbed-wire compound, a honked horn, a gate that opened and closed behind the car, a second gate, and finally a run-down exterior giving way to a surprisingly polished interior — televisions, desks, a busy office floor.



There, in the office of a man identified only as “Mr. Hill,” security guards produced strongboxes belonging to Peter and Ben. Each man opened his own box with his own key, revealing, Pettle says, ten kilos in one and thirty in the other. Then two more men — introduced as Moses and Patrick — arrived unannounced with five kilos of their own.



Pettle agreed to take five kilos total, combined from all three sources, with Peter — who held a diplomatic passport — set to fly back to Canada with him and the gold. The running total by then was roughly $68,000.



Then came the final charges: $6,000 to expedite an “expired” export license, and additional tax for the extra kilos, bringing the total to nearly $29,000 more. Robert wired it. Everyone, Pettle recalls, seemed satisfied when the meeting ended.



The Passport Standoff



Afterward, Peter asked for the one kilo Pettle was still holding as collateral. Pettle refused — it was the only tangible thing he had for his money. He offered a trade instead: the gold for Peter’s passport, so that if he’d been cheated, he’d at least have a photograph to bring to authorities. Peter refused and left angrily.



Days later, a man named Elijah Teahjay — who Pettle says “looked the most legitimate” of everyone he’d met — invited him to a second compound, even more polished than the first, complete with flags and a formal reception area. There, armed guards wheeled in a case holding what Pettle estimates was 300 kilos of gold and told him to take his pick. The new deal: $24,000 up front, $110,000 per kilo on delivery in Canada, payable within 72 hours. The gold, Elijah assured him, would simply be handed to him after customs. “We do it all the time,” he said.



The Man in the Yellow Shirt



The unraveling began with a knock at Pettle’s hotel room door. A representative from Noble Shipping arrived unannounced with an official-looking export license and a new tax bill — $21,000, then, minutes later, a second bill for $27,500. When Pettle tried to photograph the documents, the man blocked his camera, insisting they weren’t his to keep, even though he’d paid for them.



Suspicious, Pettle called Elijah and sent him a photo of the receipt, threatening to involve police if it wasn’t legitimate. Within minutes, a large man in a yellow shirt appeared at the hotel, identifying himself as “Todd” — Liberia’s minister of minerals, he claimed, though he carried no badge, only a worn business card.



What followed, Pettle says, played out “like the end of a lousy movie”: Todd confronted the Noble Shipping representative in front of him, questioned him about the missing export license, and asked Pettle to get into a car. Pettle refused to get in fully, kept one foot on the pavement, and agreed only to meet again the next morning. Within minutes of that encounter ending, his phone lit up with calls from what felt like a dozen different people connected to the scheme, all anxious to know why he’d mentioned police.



Getting Out



By his final night in Liberia, Pettle believed he might be in real danger. As far as the network knew, he’d genuinely gone to authorities. A woman named Grace — another gold contact who’d surfaced days earlier — offered to come collect him from the hotel. He nearly accepted, then reconsidered: if Grace was part of the same web, leaving with her might not be safe either. Instead, a hotel worker moved him quietly to a different room for the night. He slept, and the next morning, he left the country.



An Unlikely Postscript



Pettle did file a report with local police — six officers, he says, took his statement and had him sign it. What strikes him most, looking back, is what they never asked for: the names of the men involved, which he had; the passport used, which he had; or a single phone number from the dozens who called him during the ordeal.



“This is the beginning of a dormant complaint,” Pettle writes. But his closing line is the one that lingers: despite everything, he says his real ambition is still “to come back and bring investment to your beautiful country” — if Liberia will have him.

World.title: After 35 Years, Liberia Reopens Embassy in India
World.content:
NEW DELHI, India — Liberia has officially reopened its Embassy in New Delhi after more than 35 years without a resident diplomatic mission in India, marking a major step in efforts to strengthen bilateral relations between the two countries.

Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti is in New Delhi to formally inaugurate the Embassy on behalf of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the Government and people of Liberia.

The Liberian Embassy in India was closed more than three decades ago amid geopolitical and other challenges facing the country. Successive administrations subsequently sought to restore a permanent diplomatic presence in India, recognizing the country’s growing importance as a partner in Asia.

The reopening culminates years of efforts spanning several administrations. The Government said President Boakai’s administration has built on earlier initiatives to complete the process and restore Liberia’s resident diplomatic presence in New Delhi.

Speaking ahead of the inauguration, Minister Nyanti described the reopening as both a diplomatic milestone and an opportunity to deliver practical benefits to Liberians.

“After more than three decades, Liberia once again has a permanent diplomatic home in India,” Nyanti said. “This is a major milestone for our country and a testament to President Boakai’s commitment to strengthening Liberia’s global partnerships and ensuring that our diplomacy delivers tangible results for our people.”

She also acknowledged the efforts of successive administrations that worked toward reestablishing the mission.

The reopening is particularly significant given the growing number of Liberian students pursuing education and professional training in India, as well as Liberians traveling there for medical treatment.

The resident Embassy is expected to strengthen consular services and provide more direct assistance to Liberian citizens while creating opportunities for scholarships, education, healthcare and professional capacity building.

Beyond consular services, the Embassy is expected to serve as Liberia’s principal diplomatic and economic platform in India, with a focus on attracting investment, promoting trade and private-sector partnerships, and expanding cooperation in agriculture, technology, infrastructure and healthcare.

The mission will also support Liberia’s broader economic diplomacy and national development priorities by helping mobilize technical assistance and development partnerships.

India remains an important development and economic partner for Liberia, with bilateral cooperation spanning education, health, agriculture, technology, infrastructure, capacity building, trade and private-sector development.

The Government of Liberia expressed appreciation to India for its cooperation and support in facilitating the reopening of the Embassy and said the development marks a new chapter in Liberia–India relations.

World.title: Liberia: Gongloe Demands Independent Probe Into Cocaine Crisis
World.content:
Monrovia — As Liberia grapples with the fallout from its largest-ever cocaine seizures, renowned Liberian lawyer and politician Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe has issued one of his strongest warnings yet, describing the country’s escalating narcotics problem as a national security emergency and cautioning that Liberia must not follow the path of Haiti, where criminal networks have severely weakened state authority.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

In a lengthy commentary, Gongloe called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to establish an independent Commission of Inquiry to investigate the cocaine seizures, trace the money behind the alleged trafficking network and determine whether individuals within Liberia’s security and political establishment helped facilitate the operation.

“Liberia must not become Haiti,” Gongloe declared, warning that the country could face a gradual erosion of state authority if corruption, organized crime and compromised security institutions are not confronted decisively.

Gongloe, a former standard-bearer of the Liberian People’s Party who contested the 2023 presidential election, said the scale of the cocaine seizures demonstrates that Liberia is confronting more than a conventional law-enforcement problem.

According to authorities, approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine, valued at more than US$19 million, were seized at Roberts International Airport in June. The country was subsequently rocked by the discovery of approximately 3,971 kilograms — nearly four metric tons — of cocaine, estimated to be worth about US$317 million, in the Duazon area.

Gongloe said the volume and value of the drugs point to an organized and well-financed international criminal enterprise.

“This is not the work of a few young people selling drugs on a street corner,” he said. “The sheer volume and value point to an organized and well-financed international criminal enterprise.”

He said investigators must determine who imported the drugs, who received and transported them, who provided protection, and whether anyone within the Liberian state facilitated the operation.

‘Follow the Money’

Central to Gongloe’s proposed response is a comprehensive financial investigation.

“The central principle must be simple: follow the money,” he said.

He argued that the investigation should extend beyond the cocaine itself to financial transactions, unexplained wealth, properties, businesses, bank accounts, communications, airport records, immigration records, shipping records and political relationships.

“Cocaine is the commodity. Money is the motive. Corruption is often the bridge between criminal money and legitimate institutions,” Gongloe said.

He stressed that allegations against individuals must not be treated as established facts and that anyone accused of wrongdoing must be afforded due process and presumed innocent until proven guilty.

But he said due process cannot become an excuse for government inaction.

“The rule of law does not mean that government should remain silent when credible allegations of criminal conduct reach into the highest levels of government,” he said. “The rule of law requires a fearless, impartial and professional investigation.”

Calls for Independent Commission

Gongloe acknowledged actions already taken by the Boakai administration, including reported suspensions, dismissals, arrests, charges and detentions involving individuals connected to the investigation.

He praised the administration for taking steps in the direction of accountability but said the measures remain insufficient given the magnitude of the crisis.

“Mr. President, this is not enough,” Gongloe said.

He urged President Boakai to establish a commission composed of experts in criminal investigation, narcotics trafficking, financial intelligence, forensic accounting, money laundering, organized crime, constitutional and criminal law, cybersecurity, border security and asset tracing.

The commission, he said, should have the authority to obtain documents and testimony, trace financial transactions and examine relevant communications and movements.

Its findings, he added, should be made public, subject only to legitimate national-security restrictions.

Warning About State Capture

Gongloe said Liberia should study Haiti’s experience as a warning of what could happen when criminal organizations become stronger than state institutions.

He argued that institutional collapse does not happen overnight, but through a gradual process in which corruption becomes normalized, criminal networks purchase protection, security institutions become compromised, and young people are recruited into criminal enterprises.

“A country does not wake up one morning and discover that gangs control its streets,” he said. “Institutional deterioration occurs gradually.”

He warned that Liberia must confront the warning signs before organized crime becomes entrenched.

“That is the road Liberia must refuse to travel,” he said.

Beyond Cocaine

Gongloe linked the cocaine crisis to what he described as deeper problems of governance, corruption, weak institutions, impunity and unexplained wealth.

He raised questions about several other national controversies, including the multimillion-dollar project in Foya, Lofa County, and allegations surrounding illegal mining activities along the Liberia-Guinea border.

Gongloe was careful to distinguish questions from accusations, emphasizing that he was not alleging that the Foya project was financed with drug money.

Instead, he argued that the government should provide complete transparency about the project’s financing, procurement and authorization.

“If the money is legitimate, transparency should establish that fact,” he said. “If the procurement was lawful, the records should establish it.”

He similarly called for investigations into allegations of illegal mining along the Makona River, saying illicit mineral extraction could become a corruption, revenue, border-security and national-security problem.

A Message to Boakai

Gongloe also invoked President Boakai’s 2023 campaign-era remark that he could “dance with the devil” if doing so would help him win the presidency.

He said he was not suggesting that Boakai had any agreement with drug traffickers or that the president’s statement was connected to the cocaine crisis. Instead, Gongloe used the remark as a broader warning about political compromises.

“Every compromise with corruption has a price. Every accommodation with criminality has a price,” he said.

He described the “devil” metaphorically as corruption, greed, impunity, political patronage and abuse of public office.

“The real devil in Liberia is not a supernatural being,” Gongloe said. “The real devil is corruption. The real devil is greed. The real devil is impunity.”

Youth at Risk

Gongloe said Liberia’s young population is particularly vulnerable to recruitment by international narcotics networks because of unemployment, poverty and limited economic opportunities.

He warned that drug traffickers have the financial resources to offer young people opportunities that legitimate employment cannot match.

“What happens when a young Liberian begins to believe that a drug dealer has more opportunities than a university graduate?” he asked.

He said Liberia’s response must therefore go beyond arrests and prosecutions to include education, employment, public health, youth development, criminal justice and border security.

“Arrests alone will not solve it,” he said. “We must destroy the economic ecosystem that makes narcotics profitable.”

‘No One Should Be Above the Law’

Gongloe urged the government to investigate anyone connected to the drug-trafficking network regardless of political affiliation, social status or proximity to power.

“If the evidence leads to a poor man, investigate him. If it leads to a police officer, investigate him. If it leads to a businessman, investigate him. If it leads to a minister, investigate him,” he said.

“If it leads to someone close to the President, investigate him.”

He emphasized that the objective should not be to target individuals but to establish the truth and protect the Republic.

“No one should be above the law,” he said. “Not because we want to destroy people, but because we want to save Liberia.”

‘The System Must Be Examined’

Gongloe said the eventual destruction of the seized cocaine should not mark the end of the investigation.

“The cocaine may be destroyed. The suspects may eventually be convicted or acquitted. But the system that allowed such an enormous criminal enterprise to operate in Liberia must be examined,” he said.

He called on the government to identify the facilitators, protectors and beneficiaries of the alleged trafficking network and ensure that prosecutions follow where evidence warrants.

He also urged Liberians to resist turning the crisis into another partisan political dispute.

“Do not ask first whether the matter involves the Unity Party, the CDC or the LPP,” he said. “Ask whether Liberia is safe.”

Gongloe said the crisis represents a test for the presidency, security institutions, courts, Legislature and political parties — but ultimately, a test for the Liberian nation.

“We survived civil war. We survived Ebola. We survived political instability. We must not now lose Liberia to organized crime,” he said.

His central demand to President Boakai was repeated throughout the commentary: establish an independent inquiry, follow the money, follow the evidence, and ensure that justice reaches everyone implicated.

“Liberia deserves the truth,” Gongloe said.

“The cocaine may be seized. The cocaine may be destroyed. But the lesson must not be destroyed with it.”

He concluded with a stark warning: “If we do not control the criminals, the criminals may eventually control us. If we do not defeat corruption, corruption may eventually defeat the Republic.”

“Liberia must answer those questions, and Liberia must answer them now.”

World.title: Nine Arrested in Matero Over Polling Agent Murder
World.content:
THE Zambia Police Service has confirmed multiple arrests following isolated incidents during and after the August 13 General Elections.

In Matero, Lusaka Province, nine suspects have been arrested in connection with the alleged murder of 57-year-old polling agent LOVEMORE CHISHIMA.

Mr. CHISHIMA was allegedly assaulted at Kasamba Polling Station and later died.

According to a statement issued by Inspector General of Police GRAPHEL MUSAMBA, the suspects are in police custody as investigations continue.

In a separate incident, police arrested six men allegedly found in possession of offensive weapons, 22 rounds of ammunition and a Toyota Land Cruiser.

Police say they are seeking SEAN TEMBO to assist with investigations.

Meanwhile, in Kalomo, Southern Province, one suspect was arrested following an incident in which four people were assaulted, with one victim sustaining a gunshot wound.

Police recovered a firearm and ammunition.

In Kasama, Northern Province, police are also investigating an attack on the residence of Acting Permanent Secretary BEAUTY UNDI-PHIRI, allegedly carried out by armed supporters of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity.

One suspect has since been apprehended.

Mr. MUSAMBA says although the overall conduct of the elections was peaceful, police are taking the reported incidents seriously.

He has warned against incitement, unlawful activities and the spread of false information, while urging citizens to remain calm and allow the Electoral Commission of Zambia to professionally manage and announce the election results.

World.title: ECZ lifts suspension, sets 22:00 for first results after security review
World.content:
ECZ lifts suspension, sets 22:00 for first results after security review

The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has lifted, with immediate effect, its suspension of the counting and announcement of results in the 2026 general election, and says the first set of results will be announced at 22:00 tonight.

ECZ Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis told a press briefing on Friday that a review of the security situation, carried out in consultation with law enforcement agencies, found that the threat to the electoral process had been contained and that measures were now in place to allow counting to resume.

The Commission had earlier suspended counting and the announcement of results nationwide after reports of violence directed at polling staff and, in some instances, the theft of marked ballot papers from ballot boxes. That suspension was to be reviewed within 24 hours depending on the security situation.

“Following a review of the security situation and consultations with the relevant law enforcement agencies, I am pleased to inform you and to inform the nation that the security threat to the electoral process has been contained,” Zaloumis said.

She said polling had been successfully conducted at all polling stations across the country, with the last station closing in the early hours of Friday at 02:00.

“We therefore wish to advise all stakeholders that the suspension of the counting and announcement of results has been lifted, with immediate effect,” she said.

Zaloumis appealed to political parties, candidates, their supporters and members of the public to remain peaceful and allow polling staff to work without interference, intimidation or violence. She said the safety of polling staff, the security of electoral materials and the integrity of the process remained paramount, and that law enforcement agencies would continue providing security as counting and the announcement of results proceed.

She reminded the nation that official results are only those announced by the ECZ in accordance with prescribed procedures, and warned candidates against self-declaration.

“It is an offence under Section 89(1) of the Electoral Process Amendment Act No. 32 of 2021 for any person without lawful authority to announce and declare the results of an election,” she said, urging all presidential and other candidates to desist from declaring themselves winners and to allow the Commission to complete its constitutional duty of counting, verifying and announcing results.

Zaloumis thanked Zambians for their patience and cooperation, acknowledged the work of law enforcement in maintaining order, and commended ECZ staff for their commitment to duty. She said the Commission would continue to update the nation as the process progresses, and that stakeholders were invited to join at 22:00 as the first results begin to stream in.

The suspension, and now its lifting, come after opposition leader Brian Mundubile declared himself the winner of the presidential election on Friday, citing his alliance’s parallel vote tabulation, a claim that remains a Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance position rather than an official result. President Hakainde Hichilema had called on Zambians to remain calm as the count continued.

World.title: HICHILEMA SAYS EARLY ELECTION RESULTS ENCOURAGING
World.content:
PRESIDENT HAKAINDE HICHILEMA says he has continued to receive encouraging results following yesterday’s voting.

President HICHILEMA says he has also received reports of peace, unity and solidarity across the country as the counting process continues.

In a statement posted on his Facebook page, President HICHILEMA has urged Zambians to remain peaceful, patient and patriotic while awaiting the official results from the Electoral Commission of Zambia — ECZ.

Meanwhile, UPND National Management Committee representative MULAMBO HAIMBE says early indications from tallying centres are encouraging for President HICHILEMA.

Mr. HAIMBE says reported trends point to a strong performance for the incumbent, with high voter turnout recorded in Southern, Western and North-Western Provinces.

He says the picture in Central Province is favourable, while the party is also seeing gains in Northern Province.

However, Mr. HAIMBE has stressed that the information being shared represents early indications and not official election results.

He says only the ECZ has the constitutional authority to declare the winner of the presidential election.

Mr. HAIMBE has further cautioned political parties and members of the public against circulating unverified claims of victory, saying the ECZ should be allowed to complete the process of collation, verification and announcement of results.

The UPND has since called on citizens to exercise patience and restraint and respect the conclusion of the democratic process.

World.title: Ex-ZBF boss Chileshe hails bronze medal winning boxers
World.content:
Former Zambia Boxing Federation President Thomas Chileshe has hailed Team Zambia’s boxers for securing the country’s only two medals at the just-ended Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland.

Team Zambia’s entire medal haul came from the ring, with Catherine Mwape and Emmanuel Katema, both claiming bronze.

Mwape made history as the first Zambian female boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal after reaching the semi-finals of the Women’s 54kg division. She lost to India’s Preeti Preeti.

Katema added a second bronze in the men’s 65kg category following a hard-fought semi-final defeat to England’s Patris Mughalzai.

Speaking in Ndola, Chileshe said winning at the Commonwealth Games is never easy.

“The boxers have done well. We cannot complain. Moreover, it is not easy to get a medal at the Commonwealth Games. I know we couldn’t get gold like we did in Manchester in 2002. It is not a failure, it is an achievement.”

The former ZBF chief reminded Zambians of the country’s rich boxing pedigree on the Commonwealth stage, citing past legends.

“From the archive Zambia is very strong in boxing. This is a testament and a fact about Zambia and boxing, let’s look back to the time of Lottie Mwale, Charm ‘Shuffle’ Chiteule or even the time of Kennedy Kanyanta, we are very talented in boxing.”

Zambia’s boxing history at the Games includes historic gold medals from Lottie Mwale in 1974 and recent podium finishes such as silver and bronze at Birmingham 2022.

Chileshe, however, urged the medalists not to get comfortable.

“Our boxers should not wear the pride for now until they achieve greater things. If they relax, pride will drop them down. Let them reach the sky.”

World.title: ECZ Suspends Counting and Announcement of Results
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia — ECZ — has with immediate effect suspended the counting and announcement of election results across the country.

The Commission says the decision follows reports of violence during the counting and announcement of results in some districts.

In a press release issued today, ECZ Chairperson MWANGALA ZALOUMIS said the violence has targeted polling staff and, in some cases, resulted in the theft of marked ballot papers from ballot boxes.

Mrs. ZALOUMIS said the suspension has been necessitated by the prevailing security situation and continued threats of violence.

She said the decision has been made in accordance with Section 67, Subsection 3 of the Electoral Process Act Number 35 of 2016.

The ECZ Chairperson said the Commission will review the suspension within 24 hours.

The suspension means the counting and announcement of results will remain on hold until the Commission makes a further determination.

World.title: Shibuyunji election results pour in
World.content:
Elections results from 18 out of 33 polling stations for Mwembezhi East Constituency in Shibuyunji district have been verified and announced.

As of 08:00 hours today, the totaling centre had received results from Makombwe, Nampeya, Nampundwe, Sala and Chikonka Ward respectively.

ZANIS reports that Mwembezhi East Returning Officer Sitali Muwanei said so far United Party for National Development (UPND) Presidential candidate Hakainde Hichilema has garnered 6, 175 votes followed by National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Peace (NRPUP) candidate Brian Mundubile with 912 votes.

The returning officer noted that only results for Presidential candidates have been verified and announced.

Mr Muwanei explained that results are still coming from the remaining polling stations and will be announced as they arrive.

He has urged stakeholders to exercise patience as they wait for results.

World.title: Mbala receives poll results
World.content:
bala Central Constituency has continued receiving results from various polling stations following the closure of polls last night.

The totaling centre has so far received results from 25 out of the 52 polling stations in the constituency.

According to the latest figures, at Presidential level, National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) candidate Brian Mundubile is leading with 3,746 votes, while United Party for National Development (UPND) candidate Hakainde Hichilema has polled 2,857 votes.

The figures are from a total of 6,912 votes cast so far.

At Parliamentary level, NRPUP candidate Raphael Chilufya is leading with 3,954 votes, while UPND candidate Annie Namonga has polled 2,490 votes.

The Parliamentary results are from a total of 6,883 votes cast.

The totaling of results is still ongoing at the Mbala Central Constituency Totaling Centre.

World.title: ECZ announces NRPUP lead in Lusangazi
World.content:
National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Peace (NRPUP) Candidate Banda Festone has taken an early lead in the Ukwimi Ward race in Lusangazi Central Constituency after polling 785 votes from 5 of the 6 polling stations tallied, the Electoral Commission of Zambia has announced.

According to the ECZ record of proceeding at the totalling of votes announced yesterday, August 13, 2026, a total of 1,619 ballot papers were recorded covering Kasangazi Primary School-01, Sandwe Local Court-01, Songovwa Community School-01, Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-01 and Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-02 centres.

Of the total votes cast, 26 ballots were rejected.

Festone Banda, led the race with 785 votes, followed by United Party for National Development (UPND)’s Phiri Enala with 655 votes, while Citizens First’s Mapeti Paul garnered 106 votes.

Mr Banda got his highest figure at Kasangazi Primary School-01 with 238 votes and at Songowe Community School-01 with 190 votes.

He also polled 160 votes at Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-01 and 149 votes at Ukiwimi ‘A’ Primary School-02.

Ms Phiri led at Sandwe Local Court-01 with 138 votes and at Songowe Community School-01 with 183 votes.

Mapeti Paul’s highest return was 94 votes at Songowe Community School-01.

The totalling of results for the remaining one polling station in Ukwimi Ward is expected to be complete later today in accordance with The Electoral Process Act, No. 35 of 2016 and The Electoral Process (General) Regulations, 2021.

Final results for Ukwimi Ward Councillor will be announced once all 6 polling stations have been tallied and verified.
