World.title: Luigi Mangione admits killing healthcare CEO while pleading guilty to federal charges
World.content:
The man charged with gunning down UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on a New York City street nearly two years ago with a 3-D printed pistol pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges in Manhattan on Friday as Thompson’s family looked on.

In his allocution to the court, Luigi Mangione, 28, revealed for the first time that in 2024 he posed as a potential investor who managed over $50 billion in assets and emailed leadership at the insurance giant to confirm the location of the investors conference so he could track Thompson’s location.

“My travel to New York and email to UnitedHealthcare was with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson,” Mangione said in his statement. “On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024, I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died.”

The admitted gunman — who is Ivy League-educated and hails from a prominent Baltimore family — said he understood his actions “would place [Thompson] in fear of death or serious bodily injury” and that “I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

Mangione also told the judge that he was driven to kill Thompson because of his experience with the healthcare system as a patient with a back injury. Prosecutors have previously said that Mangione had no personal connection to UnitedHealthcare and he was never a customer.

In his statement, Mangione mocked the healthcare industry, citing UnitedHealthcare’s reply to his investment ruse. “Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour,” Mangione said.

Thompson’s family issued a rare public statement after the plea hearing, calling it “an important step toward justice for Brian and for our family.”

“While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable,” the statement said. “Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime.”

Mangione faces a maximum sentence of life in prison and prosecutors suggested that his sentencing range under federal guidelines would be 24 to 30 years in prison. Prosecutors later clarified that they would be recommending life in prison, the steepest sentence available.

He will be sentenced at a separate hearing on Dec. 18 and the final sentence will be determined by the judge, who has full discretion.

His federal court guilty plea is expected to kick off a double jeopardy fight in state court where he still faces murder charges and the possibility of life in prison. Mangione’s defense is expected to argue that the cases cover the same alleged conduct and that proceeding with a state court trial would amount to a legal violation.

“Since December 2024, the Manhattan D.A.’s Office has been tirelessly preparing to pursue a trial conviction in New York State Supreme Court for the alleged cold-blooded murder of Brian Thompson,” a spokesperson for the Manhattan District Attorney’s office said following the federal hearing. “While federal sentencing is pending, we are prepared to litigate the defense motions. The Manhattan D.A.’s Office remains committed to seeking justice for Mr. Thompson and his family.”

Following the guilty plea, Mangione’s lawyer Karen Friedman Agnifilo said, “We just filed our motion in state court explaining why the state charges must be dismissed under New York’s double jeopardy protections.”

She also discussed Mangione’s rationale.

“As Luigi explained in court today, he endured years of severe debilitating pain following a broken back while struggling to navigate our healthcare and health insurance systems,” Friedman Agnifilo said.

“He believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life,” the attorney added.

The upcoming double jeopardy fight could stall proceedings in New York Supreme Court where he’s set to stand trial Sept. 8. It could also lead to litigation in an appeals court.

In court, Mangione directly answered a standard set of questions from U.S. District Court Judge Margaret Garnett. He said “yes” to whether he understood his right to a jury trial. He also confirmed that he knew he would lose the right to vote, own a firearm and would no longer be eligible to serve on a jury.

He also said he had never been treated for mental illness and that he was clear-headed but that he had taken an antidepressant as a sleep aid in recent days.

Thompson’s family arrived in the courtroom shortly before the proceeding was set to begin. Pat Thompson, the victim’s mother, was in the front row along with other relatives and executives from UnitedHealthcare.

The Thompsons have largely remained out of the public eye since the executive was murdered. Fervent followers of Mangione are believed to be responsible for threats to Thompson’s family in the wake of his killing.

Newly installed Manhattan U.S. Attorney James McDonald was in the front row and lawyers for Mangione filed into the courtroom early.

“While the defendant pled guilty, our office does not have a plea agreement with him,” McDonald said outside the courthouse after Mangione’s plea. “Instead, he pled open, which means he pled guilty to all pending counts in the indictment. There are no accommodations or concessions, and we are free to seek the maximum penalty under the law.”

“The result achieved today now allows our office to seek the maximum penalty allowed, life imprisonment, which, as I’ve conveyed to Mr. Thompson’s family, is what we intend to seek,” McDonald added.

Mangione was charged with two federal counts — interstate stalking resulting in death and stalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death. The charges carry a maximum penalty of life in prison and are separate from the state allegations, which include second-degree murder and firearms crimes.

01:35 What Luigi Mangione could gain from plea negotiations 00:00 00:00

For now, there is still a trial scheduled in state court next month. The parties were still awaiting word late Friday afternoon on whether it will be delayed.

When Mangione was first charged in the federal case, he faced a total of four counts, including using a firearm to commit murder, which carried a maximum penalty of death. A judge dismissed that charge earlier this year, along with a second charge.

The brazen killing of Thompson — a father of two who led the nation’s largest healthcare insurer — put a spotlight on the country’s health insurance industry and widespread frustration over denied claims.

Mangione was arrested at a Pennsylvania McDonald’s restaurant Dec. 9, 2024, five days after the killing.

Among the pieces of evidence found by authorities in Mangione’s backpack was a notebook that detailed his apparent grievances against the industry. At the scene, authorities found a bullet and two shell casings that had the words “delay,” “deny,” “depose” written on them.

Mangione’s attorneys had sought to bar the notebook from being introduced as evidence at his trials, arguing authorities obtained it during an illegal search. Judges in both cases rejected that argument.

World.title: In an apparent shift, Vance says lowering oil prices is ‘goal No. 1’ of Iran war
World.content:
Keeping gas prices low is now the United States’ “goal No. 1” in the Iran war, Vice President JD Vance has said, as Washington threatened an indefinite naval blockade and signaled it would soon intensify economic pressure on Tehran.

The comments appeared to be the latest shift in the public rationale for the conflict, with Vance ranking Iran’s nuclear ambitions second.

The vice president’s remarks came as the Trump administration embraced a long-term effort to inflict more damage on the Islamic Republic, despite growing signs of strain on American forces and domestic pressure ahead of the midterm elections.

President Donald Trump has suggested a shift away from military force in favor of “low-keying it” with economic pressure. That followed a deadly cycle of tit-for-tat exchanges that produced no clear resolution and depleted U.S. reserves of missile interceptors.

Oil and gas prices spiked worldwide after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. Markets have since calmed since that early peak, but prices are still significantly higher than before the conflict and rose again early Friday after the most recent remarks from Vance and others.

“I know that oil is down today and it’s way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict,” Vance told Fox News on Thursday, before the latest uptick. “That’s goal No. 1 — keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country.”

He added that “obviously goal No. 2 is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.” Tehran insists it has no desire to develop one.

Trump and his team have offered various reasons for conflict with Iran, initially saying they wanted to support mass anti-government protests, before prioritizing a desire to defang Iran’s nuclear program and even topple the regime.

World.title: Woman arrested and facing felony charges in World War II Memorial vandalism case, DOJ says
World.content:
A woman accused of vandalizing the World War II Memorial has been arrested in Washington, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro announced Friday.

Melissa L. Farris is facing two felony charges in federal court, Pirro said on social media. Court documents show Farris is facing a count of willfully injuring or committing a depredation against property of the United States as well as a count of destruction of a veterans memorial.

00:17 World War II Memorial vandalized with spray paint and bubbles 00:00 00:00

“Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom. Those Americans include my father and grandfather,” Pirro wrote.

The memorial was vandalized Thursday with bubbles filling the fountain and graffiti that appeared to read “Clean hands dirty $.”

The suspect appears to have livestreamed the incident on Facebook on an account under her name.

A video posted to Facebook that went live around 2 p.m. ET Thursday shows a woman shaking a can of spray paint and then spray-painting the memorial.

“It was me. I’m doing it. I did it. It’s on camera,” the woman, whom authorities identified as Farris, said in the Thursday livestream.

Another livestream posted Friday morning appears to show the woman identified as Farris turning herself in.

Vandalism can be seen at the World War II Memorial in Washington on Thursday. Tyler M. Andrews / The Washington Post via Getty Images

Law enforcement responded to a call of a disorderly person Thursday, after which a U.S. park ranger observed the woman later identified as Farris flee the area, U.S. Park Police Detective Christopher Edmund wrote in an affidavit. The affidavit said a U.S. Park Police officer then recognized the suspect as someone they arrested in connection with unlawful camping on federal property on Monday. Farris had a Kentucky driver’s license when she was arrested on the camping charge, the affidavit said.

The arrest comes after Pirro’s office made the call to drop a case against former Olympic canoeist David “Davey” Hearn in connection with an incident at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a decision that drew President Donald Trump’s ire.

Pirro’s office said that the damage to the Reflecting Pool was “the result of flawed installation.” A judge dismissed the charge against Hearn but had not yet decided whether to ban Pirro’s office from bringing charges against Hearn in the future.

Trump denounced the vandalism in a post on Truth Social, connecting the damage at the World War II Memorial with the Reflecting Pool saga.

“Our beautiful World War II Memorial was just hit by Spray Painting Vandals. THERE CAN BE NO GREATER INSULT TO THOSE AMERICAN HEROES WHO DIED IN WORLD WAR II. First the Reflecting Pool, now this,” Trump wrote in a post Friday. “We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???”

The Friends of the National World War II Memorial said in a statement that the location is “a sacred place of remembrance—a place where veterans, families, students, and visitors from across our nation and around the world come to reflect on the courage, sacrifice, unity, and service of a generation that helped preserve freedom.”

The Interior Department, which oversees the two monuments and other historic sites, said the vandalism was “an utter disgrace and will not be tolerated.”

World.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to allow White House ballroom construction to continue
World.content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Friday asked the Supreme Court to allow him to continue construction of a sprawling ballroom adjacent to the White House.

The emergency application follows an Aug. 7 ruling by an appeals court in Washington upholding a federal judge’s decision that would block aboveground work on site while litigation moves forward.

“If allowed to go into effect, the injunction would wrongfully install a single district judge as sole arbiter of what further construction is ‘strictly necessary’ to protect the safety of the President, his family, staff members, and visitors to the White House, including foreign dignitaries, and presidents and prime ministers of other countries,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer said in the filing.

The appeals court decision has yet to go into effect, meaning construction continues while the Supreme Court decides what to do next. The deadline for the justices to act is Aug. 21, with Sauer asking the court to act immediately.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld an injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Richard Leon.

Leon said that the White House could move forward with below-ground construction of security and medical facilities, but not the ballroom itself.

The administration immediately appealed, and his ruling has not gone into effect.

One key issue in the case is whether the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which brought the underlying lawsuit, has legal standing to sue based on its members being harmed by construction of a building they object to on aesthetic grounds.

The group’s claim rests on a declaration made by member Alison Hoagland, a long-standing preservationist who lives in Washington and serves on the organization’s board of trustees.

She regularly walks near the White House and said she would “suffer both professional and personal injuries, including to my aesthetic, cultural and historical interests, if a ballroom of the proposed form and scale were constructed.”

In the new filing, Sauer said the project is now 65% complete, with a superstructure five stories deep and 70 feet high. A 250-person crew is working 20 hours a day, seven days a week, he said.

No taxpayer funds are being used, Sauer added, with the project funded by $400 million in private donations. (Comcast Corp., the parent company of NBCUniversal, is one of the donors.)

Sauer dismissed Hoagland’s claim, saying that the “subjective displeasure of an offended observer does not amount to concrete injury.”

The trust on Friday issued a statement saying that the administration is “actively attempting to outrun the courts” by continuing construction, and called for the Supreme Court to reject Trump’s request.

World.title: Jason Arday, ex-Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism, found dead week after resigning
World.content:
A former Cambridge professor was found dead at his London home on Friday, one week after he resigned from his position at the esteemed university following accusations of plagiarism.

Jason Arday, 41, became the youngest Black professor at Cambridge when he was hired as professor of sociology of education in 2023.

London’s Metropolitan Police said it responded to a report of a man found unresponsive inside a property at 3:12 p.m. on Friday, and the man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been notified and are being supported by officers, police told NBC News, without naming Arday.

Authorities said his death is being treated as “unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.”

The case is under investigation.

University of Cambridge Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice confirmed his passing in a statement Friday.

“We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time,” she said.

Arday was known for his neurodivergence; he had said he was diagnosed with autism as a child and was unable to speak until the age of 11. He went on to forge a path in academia as a scholar of race, inequality and education.

Arday had resigned on Aug. 5 following scrutiny over alleged plagiarism in his academic work and questions about his accomplishments.

Last month, questions regarding his qualifications were raised publicly by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the institution after critiquing diversity, equity and inclusion programs, The Associated Press reported.

In July, the Times of London also published an analysis of Arday’s 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting passages that were “identical or near-identical” to an earlier paper written by another researcher, according to the Associated Press. British media also questioned Arday’s claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($7.4 million) for charity through athletic feats, including running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.

While Cambridge initially defended Arday, on Aug. 5 it opened an investigation “following new information about Professor Arday’s qualifications and honorary appoints.”

In his resignation statement last week Arday described his tenure as “the privilege of my life to teach my students,” but conceded “the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack.”

“While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love,” he continued.

In a statement Thursday, Vice-Chancellor Prentice shared an update on the inquiry into Arday, saying the university would investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the Faculty of Education in 2022 and his time at Cambridge.

She also said she asked the university council’s deputy chair and council’s audit committee to establish terms for an independent review of all university processes that will take place alongside the probe into Arday.

In his resignation announcement, Arday said he reached a point where the “personal cost becomes too great.”

“For my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away,” he said.

In his statement, he insisted “this is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter,” and promised to return again.

Arday’s memoir, “Great and Unfortunate Things” was released earlier this week in the U.S., which chronicles his childhood — being diagnosed with autism and developmental delays at the age of 3 —to speaking by the age of 11 and reading and writing by the age of 18.

“Without romanticizing the struggle, this is a story of determination against seemingly insurmountable odds—and of a family and a small group of believers whose compassion helped him see what is possible,” a description for the book by publisher Simon & Schuster said.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

World.title: Army temporarily grounds Apache helicopter training flights after deadly crash
World.content:
The U.S. Army said Friday it is temporarily halting Apache helicopter training flights after two soldiers were killed earlier this week in a crash near Fort Hood, Texas.

"The stand-down will remain in effect until we have a better understanding of the root cause of the accident," the Army said in a statement.

The AH-64 Apache attack helicopter crashed Wednesday in a field in rural Salado, Texas, near its base in Fort Hood, the Army and local law enforcement officials said. The Army identified the deceased pilots as Chief Warrant Officer 2 Deontre T. Huey, 34, and Warrant Officer Seth L. Olmsted, 25, both Texas natives.

"You could tell this was a violent crash," said Bell County Sheriff's Office spokesperson Bill Coleman, who told reporters the helicopter did not hit any buildings, but sparked a wildfire.

The military has not specified the cause of the crash. It is not unusual for the military to order a temporary stand-down after a fatal crash, especially if the cause is still under investigation.

The aftermath of an Apache helicopter crash in Salado, Texas, on Aug. 12, 2026. Bell County Sheriff's Office

"The Army is profoundly saddened by the loss of two Soldiers in the recent AH64 Apache helicopter crash near Fort Hood, Texas," the Army said Friday. "We mourn these aviators, and our deepest condolences remain with their families, friends, and unit during this extraordinarily difficult time."

The Army has described the newest iteration of the AH-64 Apache, which has been manufactured by Boeing since the late 1990s, as "the most advanced aerial fighting vehicle in the world." The twin-engine helicopter typically seats a pilot and a co-pilot gunner, and is equipped with a rapid fire gun and can launch Hellfire missiles.

Hundreds of Apaches are operated by Army and National Guard units, and the helicopters have been used during the U.S.-Iran war. In June, an Apache that was patrolling the Strait of Hormuz was shot down by an Iranian drone, President Trump announced. The two pilots were then rescued by a sea drone.
