Article content

Often cited as an inspiration for Gothic Romance, this book is so much more. Yes, Jane Eyre does contain certain gothic elements (an old gloomy estate full of secrets, a broody handsome love interest, also full of secrets) but the strength of the novel is in singular, unforgettable character of Jane herself. Jane’s narration of her own growth from poor, unloved orphan to independent woman feels surprisingly modern. As a child she lashes out in anger at her mistreatment, as a youth she is determined to stand on her own two feet and as an adult she refuses to accept anything but full and equal love. Jane’s passion, integrity and insistence on being treated with dignity make her a very relatable and recognizable character almost two hundred years after Jane Eyre’s first publication in 1847.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: The Falklands Legislative Assembly marks 434 years since the first recorded sighting
World.content:
The Falklands Legislative Assembly marks 434 years since the first recorded sighting

14th Friday, August 2026 - 21:43 UTC Full article

The ship appears on the territory's coat of arms and gives rise to its motto, “Desire the Right.”

The Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly marked Falklands Day on Friday, the anniversary of the first recorded sighting of the archipelago, on August 14, 1592. The day was marked by raising the Falkland Islands flag and the Union flag side by side on Victory Green, in Stanley.

The sighting is credited to English navigator John Davis, who commanded the Desire, a 120-ton vessel, and came upon the then-uninhabited islands after being blown off course while attempting to round Cape Horn through the Straits of Magellan. His account was published in London in 1600 by Richard Hakluyt. The ship appears on the territory's coat of arms and gives rise to its motto, “Desire the Right.”

Davis's voyage was followed by sightings by the Englishman Richard Hawkins in 1594 and the Dutch explorer Sebald de Weert in January 1600. The first recorded landing did not take place until 1690, when English sea captain John Strong came ashore at Bold Cove, near present-day Port Howard.

In its statement, the Assembly described the date as an occasion to reflect on the territory's history and future and on Falkland Islanders “as a people.” The text places immigration at the center of that identity: it holds that today's residents are families and individuals from across the world who put down roots in the Islands, and describes that process as “a thread that runs unbroken through our history,” from the earliest settlers to those who arrive and settle today. The community, it adds, is “diverse, resilient, and proud of its home.”

The statement closes by defining the day as a moment to reflect on “our heritage and our identity as a people with our own culture, way of life, and the right to determine our own future.”

Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the archipelago, which has been administered by the United Kingdom since 1833. In the referendum held in March 2013, residents voted overwhelmingly to retain their status as a British overseas territory. The population stands at around 3,660, according to the 2021 census.

Falklands Day was once the territory's national day, but ceased to be a public holiday in 2002, when the Executive Council moved the day off to reinstate Peat Cutting Monday, on the first Monday of October. As the date of greatest symbolic weight it has largely been displaced by Liberation Day on June 14, which commemorates the end of the 1982 conflict.

World.title: A year from the presidential vote, Argentina's parties begin to define alliances
World.content:
A year from the presidential vote, Argentina's parties begin to define alliances

14th Friday, August 2026 - 10:43 UTC Full article

With little more than a year to go before Argentina's presidential elections of October 2027, the governing party and the main opposition force began this week to realign their positions. La Libertad Avanza, the party of President Javier Milei, resumed talks with former president Mauricio Macri's PRO, while the various currents of Peronism agreed a truce aimed at blocking the electoral reform the government is promoting.

Macri and the general secretary of the presidency, Karina Milei, held a telephone conversation of around thirty minutes on Monday, their first in more than nine months. On Thursday, delegates from both forces met for two hours at the Casa Rosada: Cristian Ritondo and Fernando de Andreis for PRO, and Cabinet Chief Diego Santilli together with lawmakers Martín and Eduardo Menem for the government.

The outcome was the creation of a joint political table that will meet every two weeks, and a statement in which both sides said they shared “the conviction that Argentina cannot fall back into the hands of populism.” There is as yet no national electoral alliance. Macri has said PRO will field its own candidate in 2027 and is already promoting former economy minister Hernán Lacunza. Convergence appears strongest in Buenos Aires province.

Karina Milei has a hand in drawing up electoral lists, which gives weight to her role in the negotiations. The governing party is also holding talks with governors in around ten provinces. La Libertad Avanza won the presidency in 2023 without a single provincial governorship, an unprecedented situation in Argentine history.

The main territorial contest of 2027 will be Buenos Aires province, the country's most populous, governed by the Peronist Axel Kicillof. La Libertad Avanza opened on Thursday the premises that will serve as the base for its provincial campaign, and one of its provincial figures, Sebastián Pareja, pointed to Santilli as the likely candidate to face Kicillof.

On the opposition side, Kicillof, lawmaker Máximo Kirchner and former presidential candidate Sergio Massa met for three hours on Wednesday. They agreed to defend the open, simultaneous and compulsory primaries known as PASO, which the government seeks to scrap alongside changes to party financing. The mechanism allows all parties to settle their candidacies on the same polling day; without it, Peronism would lose the tool it uses to resolve internal divisions, and building an opposition alliance would become harder.

Participants in the meeting warned, according to the newspaper Página 12, that those backing the removal of the primaries would have to answer for making Milei's continuity easier. The message was aimed at Peronist governors of northern provinces who tend to side with the government in Congress.

According to the latest Opinaia survey, 55% of Argentines would vote for Milei or would consider doing so, seventeen points above those who would lean towards a Kirchnerist candidate.

World.title: Argentina restricts access to an Andean plain after damage caused by a pickup truck
World.content:
Argentina restricts access to an Andean plain after damage caused by a pickup truck

14th Friday, August 2026 - 08:40 UTC Full article

Authorities in the Argentine province of San Juan will keep access to Pampa del Leoncito restricted until the end of the month, after a vehicle drove across the white clay plain, located at 1,500 meters above sea level at the foot of the Andes, despite a ban on traffic, leaving ruts up to 25 centimeters deep.

The episode took place on Saturday night. According to the authorities' reconstruction, a 46-year-old physician from the neighboring province of Mendoza travelled around a kilometer and a half before the pickup became stuck in the mud. He tried to reverse between 200 and 300 meters, used a ladder in an attempt to free it and, failing to do so, abandoned the vehicle and left on a motorcycle he was carrying in the truck bed, leaving fresh marks on the ground.

Traffic had already been limited before the incident because of rainfall in the area. The surface, made up of silts and clays of saline origin, loses consistency when saturated with water and deforms under the weight of vehicles and people. Once the ground hardens again, the ruts become part of the landscape and cannot be erased with machinery without causing greater damage.

The mayor of Calingasta, Sebastián Carbajal, estimated the deepest marks could take close to a century to disappear, a projection based on earlier damage rather than a technical report on this case. San Juan's director of cultural heritage, Gladys González, called the events “very regrettable” and agreed the deterioration exceeds that caused by previous breaches involving quad bikes.

The driver came forward voluntarily to give his account, provided an address and was released. He said he had not seen the signage in the dark and maintained he was unaware of the restrictions. The justice of the peace handling the case, Andrés Troche, said the man knows the area and crossed it at around 8pm on Saturday. No formal charges have been brought and there has been no conviction. The vehicle remains in place under National Gendarmerie custody, with no attempt to remove it until water levels fall.

Provincial law provides for a fine of up to 1.5 million pesos, around a thousand dollars, an amount Carbajal considers insufficient. The mayor said he would seek to refer the complaint to the criminal courts and to submit a bill to the provincial legislature to strengthen protection of the area. At least three other breaches have been recorded in recent years.

Pampa del Leoncito, also known as Barreal Blanco, is around 12 kilometers long and occupies the bed of a lagoon that dried up some 10,000 years ago. Since 2002 it has formed part of El Leoncito National Park, the first in Argentina whose official mission includes protecting the night sky. Its more than 300 clear nights a year prompted the installation of two internationally significant astronomical observation centers.

World.title: Argentina's largest investment project aims to export Vaca Muerta gas
World.content:
Argentina's largest investment project aims to export Vaca Muerta gas

13th Thursday, August 2026 - 22:46 UTC Full article

The project seeks to turn gas from the Vaca Muerta formation, in Neuquén province, into liquefied natural gas exports

Argentina's majority state-owned oil company YPF confirmed on Thursday that it has filed an application for the Argentina LNG project to join the Large Investment Incentive Regime (RIGI). The venture, developed alongside Italy's Eni and the Emirati company XRG, contemplates an estimated outlay of 51 billion dollars over its full life, the largest figure submitted so far under the scheme.

The project seeks to turn gas from the Vaca Muerta formation, in Neuquén province, into liquefied natural gas exports. Its design includes gas production in Neuquén, dedicated transport infrastructure, processing plants, liquids fractionation trains and two floating liquefaction units with a combined capacity of 12 million tonnes a year, which will operate off the coast of Río Negro, in the San Matías Gulf, from 2031. The consortium plans to scale up to 18 million tonnes.

“We are talking about a growth platform that will generate employment, technological development, local suppliers and an unprecedented international position for our country,” said Horacio Marín, YPF's chairman and chief executive, in the company's statement, which described joining the scheme as “a fundamental step.”

The RIGI, created under the Ley Bases, grants long-term legal, tax, customs and foreign exchange stability, conditions the company considers essential to attract international financing. The largest project filed under the scheme until now was LLL Oil, at 25 billion dollars, in May.

The investment plan foresees some 5 billion dollars for the initial exploration and drilling phase, and 29 billion over the next five years to bring the two floating units into operation, of which 24 billion corresponds to infrastructure: industrial complexes, dedicated pipelines and port facilities. The company estimates export revenues of close to 10 billion dollars a year over twenty years.

A substantial portion of the financing will be structured through project finance backed by long-term export contracts with investment-grade buyers. JP Morgan is acting as arranger. The first stage amounts to 15.5 billion dollars and, according to Marín, 47 banks submitted offers worth 2.4 times the amount sought.

The company holding the blocks was set up with YPF holding 36% of the capital and Eni and XRG 32% each. XRG is the international investment arm of ADNOC, Abu Dhabi's state oil company. Eni, which leads engineering on the development, placed the final investment decision towards the end of 2026 and described the project as a global leader in liquefied natural gas.

During the construction stage, planned between 2026 and 2030, YPF calculates some 20,000 annual jobs including direct, indirect and induced positions, peaking at up to 40,000 in the third year, and around 8,000 during the operational phase. Contracting of domestic suppliers is estimated at 15 billion dollars.

World.title: Brazil: Two days before the deadline, Bolsonaro's party cannot register Flávio as candidate
World.content:
Brazil: Two days before the deadline, Bolsonaro's party cannot register Flávio as candidate

13th Thursday, August 2026 - 22:34 UTC Full article

“You saw that they falsified my party affiliation. The system will try everything to stop me, but it will not succeed, because God is in command,” Flávio Bolsonaro said

Brazil's Liberal Party was unable on Thursday to file Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's presidential candidacy with the Superior Electoral Court, after the electoral system recorded him as a member of a different party. The deadline for submitting candidacies expires on Saturday at 7pm.

A certificate issued by the court at 11:13 on Thursday listed the senator as a regular member of the Missão party since Wednesday, August 12, and recorded his departure from the Liberal Party on the same date. Official records had until then shown continuous membership of the PL since November 2021. The discrepancy blocked the registration procedure. The campaign's legal team also reported that the party temporarily lost credentialed access to the platform used to submit data to the court.

The Superior Electoral Court said in a statement that the change did not result from a breach of its affiliation system but from improper use of the tool by someone holding access credentials, and opened an investigation. The certificate itself specifies that affiliation data is entered into the Filia system under the parties' own responsibility and that the record carries “only a relative presumption of veracity.”

Flávio Bolsonaro released a video on social media. “You saw that they falsified my party affiliation. The system will try everything to stop me, but it will not succeed, because God is in command,” he said. His team requested immediate correction of the record and announced it would ask the Federal Police to open an investigation. The change was reversed hours later.

Missão, whose president and presidential candidate is Renan Santos, said in a statement it had been the victim of a fraudulent affiliation attempt. The party said its own system detected the irregularity and tried to cancel it the same day, a request the court rejected, and announced it would provide authorities and the press with a report containing access logs, emails and IP addresses. “The last thing we want is Flávio Bolsonaro affiliated to Missão,” Santos told the Metrópoles website.

This is not the first such episode. In an earlier case, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva appeared registered as a Liberal Party member in the electoral system. The police investigation concluded the change had been made by a 13-year-old who did not breach the system, according to the same outlet.

By Thursday, six presidential candidacies had been registered, among them that of Santos, who polls at around 3%. Campaigning officially begins on Sunday, with Lula holding an event in São Bernardo do Campo, in greater São Paulo, and Flávio Bolsonaro at Copacabana beach in Rio de Janeiro. The most recent CNT/MDA poll puts the president on 48% against the senator's 39.1% in a potential runoff.

World.title: Colombia faces reconstruction with 96% of the year's debt quota already used
World.content:
Colombia faces reconstruction with 96% of the year's debt quota already used

13th Thursday, August 2026 - 22:31 UTC Full article

De la Espriella said the country is going through “the most complex fiscal crisis in its entire history” and announced that the emergency will allow the creation of the so-called Fondo Milagro

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella declared an economic emergency on Wednesday to address the consequences of Monday's magnitude 7.4 earthquake in the west of the country, against a backdrop of fiscal constraints that will shape how reconstruction is financed.

The outgoing government used 96% of the domestic debt issuance quota set for this year, an unprecedented proportion in a presidential transition, where the norm was to leave around 30% available for the successor, according to calculations by economist Alejandro Rojas of Banco de Bogotá. The current budget also faces a shortfall of more than 30 trillion pesos, some 9.375 billion dollars.

De la Espriella said the country is going through “the most complex fiscal crisis in its entire history” and announced that the emergency will allow the creation of the so-called Fondo Milagro, intended to channel domestic and international contributions towards rebuilding hospitals, schools, housing, roads and airports. “The emergency will have to include economic reactivation measures,” he said at his first press conference since taking office, at which he took no questions.

The measures announced include the state covering utility bills for affected families, rent subsidies, tax and financial relief, support for traders and small businesses, and assistance for the most vulnerable households. Finance Minister Miguel Gómez Martínez had told congressional economic committees of the possibility of taking out a World Bank loan of up to 450 million dollars and of postponing personal income tax payments by several weeks.

Wednesday's official toll stands at 265 dead, 3,494 injured, 496 missing and 25,872 families affected, with 1,136 homes destroyed, 8,357 damaged and 35 health centers hit. The figures are provisional.

The United States Geological Survey estimates the most likely losses at between one and ten billion dollars, although its upper range contemplates an impact of up to 7% of gross domestic product, equivalent to some 40.6 billion dollars. Gómez had set out to cut state spending by 20 trillion pesos this year, close to 6 billion dollars, a target reconstruction is likely to postpone. “Some of the tax cuts the government wanted will probably have to be put off, and a discussion about additional revenue may even have to be brought to the table,” said José Ignacio López, president of the think tank Anif.

A study by the International Monetary Fund covering 96 emerging economies between 2012 and 2023 concludes that markets do not penalize the earthquake itself but the institutional capacity to respond. Sovereign spreads tend to rise and stay elevated in countries with weaker state capacity, an effect that appears two months after the event and can exceed 60 basis points by the fifth month. In countries that respond effectively, the spread remains stable or even falls.

The declaration of economic emergency temporarily empowers the executive to issue decrees with the force of law and is subject to review by the Constitutional Court. In April the court struck down the emergency decreed by Gustavo Petro, though in different circumstances, after a tax reform failed in Congress. It has, however, upheld the mechanism following the 1999 Eje Cafetero earthquake, the 2010 floods and the 2017 Mocoa landslide.

World.title: Disapproval of Orsi's government climbs to 57% in the third quarter, Opción finds
World.content:
Disapproval of Orsi's government climbs to 57% in the third quarter, Opción finds

13th Thursday, August 2026 - 10:16 UTC Full article

The breakdown shows 30% rating the government's performance as very poor and 27% as poor, against 16% who consider it good and 3% very good

Fifty-seven percent of Uruguayans disapprove of the performance of the government led by Yamandú Orsi and 19% approve, according to the third-quarter 2026 Public Opinion Monitor released on Wednesday by the polling firm Opción. In the previous measurement the figures were 48% and 20% respectively.

The breakdown shows 30% rating the government's performance as very poor and 27% as poor, against 16% who consider it good and 3% very good. Twenty-four percent do not assess it either way and 1% did not answer. The net rating moved from -28 to -38 points.

The president's personal evaluation returns somewhat less negative figures. Twenty-two percent approve of his performance, 28% take neither view and 50% disapprove. His net rating went from -17 to -28 compared with the previous quarter. Orsi's approval is three points above the government's and his disapproval seven points lower.

The series for the term shows a sustained progression. Approval of the government's performance stood at 30% at the start of the mandate, 23% in the first quarter of 2026 and 20% in the second. Disapproval travelled the opposite path: 19%, 38% and 48%. According to the firm's analysis, the main shift lies not in the fall in support but in the contraction of the segment without a settled view, which was 51% at the beginning of the term and is now 24%.

The sharpest movement is within the governing party's own electorate. Among those who voted for the Frente Amplio in the first round of 2024, disapproval rose nine points from the previous quarter, the largest increase of the term so far, to 28%, while approval stands at 39%. Among Coalición Republicana voters, 81% disapprove and 4% approve. Those who backed other candidacies in 2024 show trends closer to opposition voters than to government supporters.

Opción argues this is the lowest level of support recorded by a Frente Amplio-led government at this point in a term. The measurement incorporates for the first time the controversy over the purchase of an official vehicle, which had not featured in the previous survey.

The poll was conducted by telephone in two stages, with 403 cases between July 16 and 20 and a further 403 between August 6 and 11, on a total sample of 806 people. The maximum margin of error is 3.5 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. On those parameters, the one-point change in approval is not significant, while the nine-point jump in disapproval is.

World.title: Lula's runoff lead over Flávio Bolsonaro narrows to 8.9 points, CNT/MDA poll finds
World.content:
Lula's runoff lead over Flávio Bolsonaro narrows to 8.9 points, CNT/MDA poll finds

13th Thursday, August 2026 - 09:03 UTC Full article

In the second-round scenario, Lula takes 48% of voting intentions against 39.1% for the Liberal Party senator

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva holds an 8.9-point lead over Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a potential runoff, according to the CNT/MDA poll released on Tuesday. The gap stood at 12.5 points in the June survey.

In the second-round scenario, Lula takes 48% of voting intentions against 39.1% for the Liberal Party senator. In June the figures were 49.3% and 36.8% respectively. The narrowing reflects both a 1.3-point decline for the president and a 2.3-point rise for the opposition candidate, variations that individually fall within the 2.2-point margin of error. The current gap between the two, by contrast, exceeds it comfortably. Blank and spoiled ballots account for 11% and undecided voters for 2%.

In the first round, Lula leads with 42.4%, virtually unchanged from June, followed by Flávio Bolsonaro on 28.7%, Ronaldo Caiado on 4%, Romeu Zema on 3.3% and Renan Santos on 2.8%. If no candidate exceeds 50% of valid votes, the two leading contenders go to a runoff, an outcome that has occurred in every Brazilian presidential election since 2002.

The poll tested other runoff scenarios, in which the president retains wider margins: 49% against Zema's 35%, 48% against Caiado's 36% and 49% against Renan Santos's 33%. Flávio Bolsonaro is therefore the rival who runs closest.

Measurements differ substantially depending on the polling firm. A Datafolha survey from mid-July put the runoff at 48% against 43%, four points above the figure CNT/MDA now attributes to the senator. In March, an AtlasIntel survey described the two as being in a technical tie.

The poll was commissioned by the National Transport Confederation and carried out by the MDA institute, with 2,002 face-to-face interviews conducted between August 5 and 9 in 140 municipalities across all regions of the country. The margin of error is 2.2 percentage points and the survey is registered with the Superior Electoral Court.

The figures come four days before the official start of campaigning for October's elections. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup and endorsed his candidacy in December. Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term.

World.title: Sargassum seaweed levels begin to drop in Quintana Roo after record peak
World.content:
Sargassum is beginning to recede from Quintana Roo beaches after peaking in June and July, but the Mexican Caribbean remains on track for one of its worst years on record.

The decline began this month and should become more pronounced in September and October, Esteban Amaro Mauricio, hydrobiologist and director of the Quintana Roo Sargassum Monitoring Network, said this week.

The arrival of the seaweed has been erratic, however. Tulum and Mahahual still have major accumulations while Playa del Carmen has seen less. Puerto Morelos, recently clear, received a significant influx this week.

At the beginning of this month, 30 beaches in northern Quintana Roo alone were on red alert for excessive sargassum. Amaro said the network’s latest monitoring report put 22 of the state’s northern beaches in red, 17 in orange, 13 in yellow, 45 in green and three free of the algae.

Tonnes on Quintana Roo beaches

Conditions had improved less in the south, where 30 beaches remained on red alert, with two on orange, three a piece on yellow and green, and two free of sargassum entirely.

About 110,000 tonnes of sargassum have been collected statewide this year, Amaro said. He projected a total of roughly 150,000 tonnes by year’s end, well above the 94,000 tonnes collected in 2025.

Amaro said sargassum arrivals should be minimal in November and December but could resume as early as January 2027, as they did this year. In previous years, the season typically began in April or May.

The scale offshore remains enormous. Monitors at one point detected as much as 54 million tonnes of the algae floating between Africa and the Gulf of Mexico, Amaro said, including 4 million to 5 million tonnes off the Mexican Caribbean (coast?) .

Approximately 5% to 10% of the sargassum nearest the coast reaches beaches, Amaro said.

Hurricanes, tropical depressions and tropical storms could disperse the algae, he said, although officials will keep containment barriers and offshore collection vessels in service.

Tourism impact

The influx has compounded pressures on tourism. Quintana Roo Tourism Minister Bernardo Cueto Riestra said Tulum hotel occupancy had fallen to 15%, its lowest level on record, while Playa del Carmen stood at 30%.

He cited the atypical sargassum arrival and reduced airline frequencies linked to fuel costs.

The problem affects about 30 countries, Amaro added. Sargassum is a natural part of Atlantic Ocean ecosystems, but since 2011, extraordinary proliferations have affected the Caribbean region, with impacts on coastal ecosystems, fisheries and tourism.

Mexico and Japan announced last week they are working to establish a joint sargassum-response program that could include Japanese ocean-monitoring technology, specialized equipment, collection vessels, satellite monitoring and technical training. One of its goals would be turning the algae into products such as fertilizer, biofuels and construction materials.

With reports from La Jornada, Prensa IBERO, Peninsular Caribbean and Reportur.us

World.title: Trump administration strips AMLO’s son of his US visa
World.content:
The U.S. government revoked the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán on Thursday, prompting the son of the former Mexican president to publish an aggressively worded letter to President Donald Trump on social media.

In the letter, López Beltrán (often referred to as “Andy” by Mexican media) went on the offensive, calling the decision “politically motivated and propagandistic, in the Hitlerian style.” He also dismissed the impact of the action, saying he has no problem not visiting the U.S. during times of “hate, racism and drug addiction.”

Andy insisted there is “no reason whatsoever” for the “crude and perverse act of villainy” against him, declaring that he is guided by “the ideals, principles and honesty instilled in me by my parents and practiced out of conviction in my political work.”

The letter also speculated that Trump could be unaware of the decision, saying that if the U.S. president were aware then it is an “arrogant” action and “demonstrates, as my father recently wrote, that you are now an apathetic leader, much different from the person he knew and dealt with.”

Andy’s father, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, served as Mexican president from December 2018 through September 2024, overlapping with Trump’s first term which extended from January 2017 through January 2021.

Andy was particularly harsh with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and undersecretary Christopher Landau, referring to the latter as “El Quitavisas” (“The Visa Taker”).

Landau, the U.S. ambassador to Mexico during Trump’s first term, earned his “Quitavisas” moniker — and proudly embraced it — due to his aggressive policy of reviewing and revoking U.S. visas for foreign citizens who in his judgment mocked U.S. figures, glorified violence or participated in political corruption.

In recent months, Landau has orchestrated a sweep that revoked visas for over 50 Mexican politicians, most of them linked to the ruling Morena party for which Andy had been the secretary of organization until resigning in July to prepare a run for office next year.

Members of the opposition National Action Party were quick to demand that the Federal Attorney General’s Office initiate an investigation into Andy’s potential involvement in fuel theft and influence trafficking, while insisting the Financial Intelligence Unit investigate his finances.

For her part, President Claudia Sheinbaum dismissed the revocation of Andy’s visa as “a politically motivated decision aimed at interfering in Mexico’s internal affairs.”

With reports from El País, Animal Político, La Jornada and The Associated Press

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico and Japan to collaborate on new sargassum-themed restaurant chain
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Embassy of Japan announced a revolutionary diplomatic initiative Monday, confirming plans to address the Caribbean sargassum crisis by launching a nationwide chain of high-end, eco-conscious restaurants centered entirely around the invasive macroalgae.

The venture, which will be called Sargassyum!, aims to rebrand the thousands of tons of brown seaweed washing ashore in Quintana Roo into a luxury dining experience. According to official project briefs, Japan will provide state-of-the-art culinary expertise in marine botany (aka phycogastronomy), while Mexico will supply the virtually limitless, self-replenishing inventory directly from the surf.

“For years, tourists have complained that sargassum ruins the iconic turquoise views of the Riviera Maya,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Fernando Morales during a press conference in the capital. “Through this strategic partnership with our Japanese allies, we are changing the narrative. Guests will no longer look at the shore and see an ecological nuisance; they will see an all-you-can-eat raw bar.”

Initial menu concepts, developed by a joint diplomatic culinary task force, feature dishes such as sargassum tempura, tacos de microalgas Ensenada-Style, and a signature tableside guacamole infused with harvest-fresh sea biomass. Project engineers confirmed that specialized Japanese sensors will monitor ocean currents to deliver live, real-time updates to restaurant kitchen monitors, ensuring the morning’s catch goes from tide line to taco plate in under 20 minutes.

Industry analysts expect the business model to achieve unprecedented profit margins due to negligible supply chain overhead. “Most restaurant chains spend millions securing reliable produce,” noted Mexico City economic analyst Sofia Delgado. “This chain features an automated, climate-driven supply chain that literally dumps tons of raw inventory directly onto the property twice a day.”

Diplomatic sources noted that while the initial rollout will focus on the popular Riviera Maya tourist corridor, future expansions may include a drive-thru model situated directly along beachfront boardwalks. Representatives from both nations expressed confidence that with sufficient lime juice and high-end branding, diners will comfortably overlook the texture and taste.

World.title: Breaking: Peso surges past 17 per dollar as the ‘super peso’ returns
World.content: Listen to this article The Mexican peso broke the 17-unit-per-dollar floor and was trading at around 16.98 per U.S. dollar in wholesale transactions early Friday before inching up to just over the 17 mark near midday. For two days, the peso had flirted with dipping below 17, a milestone that reinforces the strength of the local currency in international financial markets while also attracting investor attention. ﻿ The exchange rate Friday was 16.9965 pesos per dollar before 8 a.m. Mexico City time. According to the financial portal Bloomberg, the rate represents an appreciation of 0.20% for the peso, equivalent to a drop of 3.39 cents for the U.S. dollar. The last time the intraday exchange rate fell below 17 was on June 3, 2024, the day after the elections in which President Claudia Sheinbaum and the Morena party won in a landslide. By midday Friday, the exchange rate had risen to 17.0389 to the dollar. The Mexican currency closed on Thursday at 17.0431 pesos per “spot dollar,” appreciating by 0.13% compared to Wednesday’s close. Before Friday’s opening, the peso had gained ground against the dollar in four consecutive days — strengthening by 0.9% — and had appreciated by 5.2% on the year. According to data from Mexico’s central bank (Banco de México or Banxico), the exchange rate fluctuated between a maximum of 17.07 and a minimum of 17.03 in Thursday’s interbank market. “The return of the super peso is due to the global weakness of the dollar amid increased uncertainty in the U.S. economy,” Banamex analyst Paulina Anciola told El Universal newspaper. Other issues impacting the exchange rate include the latest U.S. consumer inflation report (indicating inflation had been momentarily contained), a global environment of lower volatility and investor expectations about the direction of monetary policy of the U.S. Federal Reserve and Banxico. Anciola also said the peso’s behavior is due to a greater global appetite for emerging market assets, as well as to the attractiveness of the long-term interest rate differential favoring Mexico. The differential is roughly 450 basis points in Mexico’s favor compared with the United States. “It would seem that the foreign exchange market has already internalized a significant part of the domestic uncertainty, both related to adjustments to the sovereign rating outlook, as well as in the trade arena in the face of the scenario of annual reviews of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement (USMCA) and so far there have been no episodes of high volatility,” he said. The private sector consensus forecasts a wholesale exchange rate of 17.90 pesos to the dollar by the end of this year, according to the latest Citigroup survey of 35 banks, brokerage firms and analysis groups. However, there is evidence that the peso is overvalued. In the most recent MND Peso Index™, which compares prices of a basket of goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas, the peso was found to be overvalued against the dollar by 2.4% in early August. With reports from Informador, La Jornada and El Universal

World.title: Sheinbaum sees ‘political meaning’ in US visa revocations: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇺🇸 270,000+ Mexicans deported since Trump’s second term began: The INM reported that 271,193 Mexicans were repatriated from the U.S. between Jan. 20, 2025 and Aug. 13, 2026 — 171,508 by land and 99,685 by air on 816 flights, with over 80% of air arrivals landing in Villahermosa or Tapachula.

🗺️ Chiapas tops deportee origins: Nearly 9% of repatriated Mexicans (23,915) are from Chiapas, followed by Guanajuato, Guerrero, Veracruz and Oaxaca.

⚠️ Visa revocations have “political meaning,” Sheinbaum says: Asked about the U.S. stripping visas from Morena officials — including AMLO’s son López Beltrán and Baja California Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila — Sheinbaum called it interference in Mexican politics, arguing the U.S. isn’t applying the same standard across Latin America.

🚫 “Nothing against the president’s son”: Sheinbaum said there is no case against López Beltrán over fuel smuggling allegations. She said that Mexico won’t shield anyone who committed a crime but also won’t open an investigation just because the U.S. revoked a visa.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Friday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum addressed issues related to Mexico’s relationship with the United States.

One was deportations of Mexicans from the United States since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House in early 2025. While the Trump administration has pursued an aggressive deportation agenda, the number of Mexicans expelled from the U.S. last year was, in fact, lower than in each of the years of the Biden administration.

Another important issue related to the Mexico-U.S. relationship that Sheinbaum spoke about on Friday morning was the U.S. government’s revocation of visas of Mexican officials affiliated with the ruling Morena party. Her remarks came after one of the sons of former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO), Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, revealed on Thursday that he had been stripped of his U.S. visa. In a letter addressed to Trump, López Beltrán claimed that the revocation of his visa was politically motivated.

The United States’ cancelation of Mexican officials’ visas adds to the current tension in the bilateral relationship, which has been strained by the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without the knowledge and authorization of the Mexican government, U.S. prosecutors’ drug trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya and other Morena party officials and the Trump administration’s decision to not renew the USMCA, among other issues.

A Morena party governor and Morena mayors are among the Mexican officials who have lost their U.S. visas. The Los Angeles Times reported in June that two other Morena governors have also “been stripped of their U.S. visas amid criminal probes,” but that reporting has not been confirmed.

López Beltrán’s revelation that his U.S. visa has been revoked is another headache for Sheinbaum given that the cancelation inevitably arouses, or increases, suspicions that the ex-president’s son — formerly a top Morena official — has engaged in criminal activities. The president owes at least some of her political success to AMLO, who was her political mentor for years.

Regarding the case against Rocha, Sheinbaum has endorsed the view of the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) that the United States hasn’t presented hard evidence that would warrant the extradition of the governor to the U.S. She reiterated that position on Friday.

More than 270,000 Mexicans deported from US during Trump’s second term

At the start of the press conference, Sheinbaum told reporters that the government would provide an update on the number of Mexicans “deported or repatriated” to Mexico from the United States during Trump’s second term in office.

She noted that some Mexicans are sent to Mexico on flights that arrive in southern Mexico or at the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA). Others, Sheinbaum acknowledged, are deported directly across the U.S.-Mexico border.

Wherever deported Mexicans arrive, “there is a place to receive them — a Mexico Embraces You space,” she said, referring to centers set up by the government to temporarily house deportees and provide them with a range of assistance and care before they set off to start new lives in Mexico.

Sergio Salomón Céspedes, director of the National Institute of Migration (INM), reported that 271,193 Mexicans were repatriated from the U.S. between Jan. 20, 2025 — the date Trump began his second term — and Aug. 13, 2026.

He said that 171,508 of the deportees entered Mexico by land while the other 99,685 flew into the country.

Céspedes said that the latter cohort arrived on 816 flights that touched down at 10 airports: Villahermosa, Tapachula, AIFA, Tulum, Mexico City, Mérida, Oaxaca, Morelia, Campeche and San Luis Potosí.

Data presented by the INM chief showed that over 80% of the deportees transported to Mexico by air arrived either in Villahermosa or Tapachula. The former city is the capital of Tabasco, while the latter is in Chiapas near the southern state’s border with Guatemala.

Céspedes also presented data that showed that 23,915 of the deportees are originally from Chiapas, a figure that represents almost 9% of the total number of Mexicans repatriated since January 2025. The next most common states of origin of deportees are Guanajuato, Guerrero, Veracruz and Oaxaca.

Sheinbaum: U.S. government’s revocation of visas has a ‘political meaning’

A reporter asked the president about the U.S. government’s cancelation of the U.S. visa of López Beltrán, a former secretary of organization for Morena who is now aiming to be elected as a federal deputy at elections next year. Among the other officials who represent Morena — the party founded by AMLO — and who have also been stripped of their U.S. visas is Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila Olmeda, who in a recently-leaked telephone conversation said she was willing to cooperate with U.S. authorities, apparently in order to avoid possible criminal charges in the United States and extradition to that country

Sheinbaum said that her opinion is that “this cancelation of visas … essentially has a political meaning because it’s not at the same level for all countries” in the region, various of which have right-wing governments that earlier this year joined a “counter cartel coalition” established by the United States.

“… We can do a review of what happens in other countries of Latin America and what happens in our country,” she said, tacitly expressing her view that Mexicans and indeed Mexico are being specifically targeted by U.S. authorities.

“This is a form of interference in Mexican politics. This is my opinion because I don’t see another reason,” Sheinbaum said.

“And who uses this [for their advantage]? The Mexican right,” she said, referring to parties such as the National Action Party.

The Mexican right, Sheinbaum added, is becoming “increasingly subservient to the United States.”

Sheinbaum: ‘There is nothing against the president’s son’

Later in the press conference, a reporter asked the president whether she had any information linking López Beltrán to an investigation into a tax evasion/fuel smuggling (huachicol fiscal) scheme.

“There is nothing against the president’s son,” Sheinbaum responded.

“If there was an FGR investigation, we, as I have said, are not going to provide cover for anyone if they committed a crime,” she said.

“But nor are we going to open an investigation because the United States takes away a visa,” Sheinbaum added.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Beyond mezcal and tequila: 5 traditional drinks with pre-Hispanic roots
World.content:
Beyond tequila and mezcal, Mexico hides a universe of traditional drinks that are little known outside of the regions where they originated. These beverages tend to have pre-Hispanic roots and are made from corn dough, featuring varied ingredients including cacao, wildflowers, fruits and more.

Indeed, there’s a lot more than meets the eye in Mexico’s gastronomy scene. Here are some of the lesser-known Mexican beverages that you’ve probably never heard of.

Pozol

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @laltic_quesosyproductos

Hailing from Mexico’s Maya region, pozol is one of the country’s most celebrated pre-Hispanic non-alcoholic beverages, still enjoyed by many today.

With a thick consistency and brownish color, this beverage was highly praised in pre-Hispanic times as a source of stamina for Indigenous travelers, providing nourishment and quenching thirst in the humid conditions of Mexico’s south.

The drink is prepared by cooking corn with lime, rinsing it, and grinding it to create a dough, which is then whisked into water until fully dissolved.

Nowadays, there are many varieties of pozol — all of them featuring an earthy flavor. The most popular types of pozol include brown pozol (with cacao), white pozol (without cacao), sweet potato pozol and sour pozol (with fermented corn).

The beverage is served cold.

Where to find it? Southern and southeastern Mexico, primarily in the markets of Chiapas, Tabasco, Veracruz, Oaxaca and the Yucatán Peninsula, including Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

Tascalate

Originally made from toasted corn, cacao, chile and achiote, Indigenous communities in pre-Hispanic times associated tascalate with religious properties and love, believing it fostered the blossoming of affection.

Following the Spanish conquistadors’ arrival in the region, new ingredients like cinnamon, annatto and piloncillo (unrefined cane sugar) were added to the mix, resulting in a sweet beverage, lightly spiced and smoky.

The drink, whose name comes from the Náhuatl taxcalatl, meaning “tortilla water,” is traditionally made by toasting tortillas or corn, which are then ground into a fine powder before they’re mixed with cocoa, cinnamon, annatto and sugar.

The resulting reddish-orange powder is then dissolved in water or milk, whisked to create a frothy texture, and served cold.

Where to find it? Despite efforts to commercialize it beyond its borders, tascalate is only produced in the southern state of Chiapas, where it is sold in markets, traditional restaurants and public squares.

Chone

Originally from southern Mexico, chone is a thick, reddish and aromatic beverage primarily made from cooked corn and a wide variety of ingredients including guajillo chile, rosita de cacao (cacao flower), achiote, pixtle (mamey seeds) and piloncillo.

Featuring sweet notes, a floral-vanilla aroma and the mild, smoky heat of the guajillo chile, chone is a celebratory drink reserved for special occasions like religious ceremonies and community gatherings.

To prepare it, corn kernels are boiled in water, ground and mixed again with water to form a light dough. This dough is returned to the heat and is later strained through a cloth napkin to achieve a finer texture.

Where to find it? Chone is only found in the state of Oaxaca, with a strong popularity in the communities of Santa María Atzompa, San Bartolo Coyotepec and Villa de Zaachila.

Tepache

The increasingly popular tepache is a lightly fermented and fizzy drink with a dominant flavor of ripe pineapple, piloncillo and spices that originated in pre-Hispanic times and was used as a medicinal elixir for the sick and frail.

With sweet and sour notes, tepache is the only alcoholic beverage on this list — albeit with less than 2% alcohol.

Indigenous communities from different parts of Mexico prepared it in the original way using tender corn, for which it was named tepatli, meaning “corn drink.” Nowadays, tepache is prepared with pineapple instead of corn, and thanks to its low alcohol content, it is thought more of as a refreshing beverage rather than an alcoholic drink.

Tepache’s preparation is so easy that it can be made at home without any special equipment: The pineapple rinds are placed in water with sugar or piloncillo, and the mixture is left to ferment for around three to five days at room temperature.

Following the fermentation process, the beverage is strained to remove the rinds and spices and is served with ice.

Where to find it? Tepache’s growing popularity means it’s relatively easy to find across the country, including in grocery shops.

Tejuino

Tejuino is a slushy, sweet and tangy drink reminiscent of a very mild, refreshing and slightly fermented corn beer.

Originally from western Mexico, tejuino is made with nixtamalized corn dough, piloncillo and water, and is served cold with lime, salt and ice. Even though it is a fermented beverage, it has nearly zero alcohol content, which is why this refreshing drink is enjoyed by children and adults alike.

The base is nixtamalized corn dough that is diluted with water, cooked like a thick porridge and mixed with piloncillo before being left to ferment for 24 hours to several days, depending on the local tradition.

This brownish drink is served with lime juice, coarse salt and ice or nieve de garrafa de limón (Mexican lime sorbet).

Where to find it? In markets and public squares of the states of Jalisco, Nayarit and Colima.

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: María Félix hated this portrait by Diego Rivera. Then it vanished
World.content:
María Félix was not happy when she received the work of art. After commissioning a portrait of herself from Diego Rivera, the legendary Mexican muralist, she had high expectations of the finished work — which, at first, were definitely not met.

Mexico’s Golden Age film icon wanted to be depicted as a Tehuana woman, with the classical headpiece and garments. However, Rivera did not agree: His beloved Frida Kahlo had already portrayed herself as such, and he had another vision for the portrait of “La Doña,” as Félix was known.

Everyone knew Diego was working on that project. With both of them at the peak of Latin American stardom, it was difficult to keep the secret. How is it possible, then, that a portrait of María Félix, hand-painted by Diego Rivera, disappeared for so many years? This is the story of a cursed painting that, as only happens in Mexico, is still missing.

A matter of artistic sympathies

It was well known that La Doña was strong-willed. Filmmakers, photographers and artists of various kinds found that she wanted to do things her way — and no other way. Even Rivera, with his long history of love affairs and alleged fame among women of the time, had difficulty working with her on this piece.

It was 1949. Rivera summoned María Félix to his studio in San Ángel, where he was working on that and other artistic projects. Upon seeing the finished work, La Doña could not hide her displeasure: It was not what she had asked for.

It wasn’t the first time Félix had asked to be portrayed. Immersed as she was in the Mexican art scene, she rubbed shoulders with majestic women, such as Leonora Carrington, Leonor Fini and Remedios Varo, the great witches of Mexican surrealism. All of them, moreover, had made portraits of La Doña who, according to the María Félix Foundation, had celebrated their work as being of global stature.

The case of Diego Rivera’s painting was very different. Although Félix wanted Rivera to portray her as a figure of national pride — the perfect Mexican woman — the muralist had other plans: He was determined to follow his own style (and leave Félix’s suggestions behind). It was no surprise, then, that the portrait struck her as abhorrent. Not only had he not painted her as a Tehuana, as she had requested, but she was also depicted half-naked with her breasts exposed. Years later, in an interview with journalist Jacobo Zabludovsky, the Mexican actress confessed that she “didn’t like Diego’s style, just as she didn’t like Frida Kahlo’s.”

The Mexican actress eventually agreed to the portrait. Only because they were friends, she told Rivera, only for that reason.

Stains of white paint

Although she accepted Rivera’s commission, María Félix wasn’t happy with the result. To avoid having her breasts exposed, according to gossip, she asked a mason to apply white paint over the lace Rivera had originally painted. The muralist never found out about this alteration, but only then did La Doña feel comfortable with the portrait. So much so, according to her foundation, that she kept it on display in her living room for years.

As a woman with an extremely high opinion of herself, La Doña was certain that Diego Rivera was in love with her. And it may well be true. Who wasn’t, back then? Strong, self-assured, lucid and talented, she captivated the Mexican art scene with her presence.

Some time after the painting was delivered, Diego Rivera asked María Félix to lend it to him for a portrait exhibition he was organizing. The actress flatly refused, knowing that she had altered the portrait without the artist’s consent.

A short time later, she sold the piece to Dr. José Álvarez Amézquita, who was then building his career in Mexican healthcare politics. What difference would it make, the actress thought. After all, she didn’t even like the portrait, and it was already causing problems at home: Her husband at the time, Alexander Berger, didn’t like the painting either. Unbeknownst to them at the moment, that purchase would cause the painting to wander for decades, until it disappeared from the map completely.

Another pop culture icon buys the painting

Dr. Álvarez Amézquita was not the last owner of the portrait Diego Rivera painted of María Félix. In the 1970s, years after Frida and Diego’s deaths, songwriter and performer Juan Gabriel bought the painting for 15 million pesos. As a devoted admirer of the actress since his youth, he could not have been happier to have the coveted painting in his personal collection.

After acquiring the painting, he wrote “María de Todas las Marías,” and even compared her to the Virgin of Guadalupe. The Mexican public forgave the blasphemy.

Like other eccentricities, the painting remained in the possession of Juan Gabriel’s family for decades. It wasn’t until his untimely death from a heart attack in 2016 that the portrait of María Félix disappeared. Amid the turmoil, confusion and grief over the icon’s loss, the artwork vanished, its whereabouts unknown for the past 10 years.

A national treasure is missing

Much of the investigation revolved around Juan Gabriel’s universal heir, Iván Gabriel. As his only recognized biological son, it was natural that his possessions would remain in his name. However, he for a time had no control over the US $45 million estate his father left — among which was María Félix’s portrait by Diego Rivera.

In 2020, with the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, a glimmer of hope emerged in the case. Lawyer Guillermo Pous claimed that the painting was in the possession of César Duarte, the controversial Mexican politician. It was never known if he actually had it.

One version suggests that Juan Gabriel’s family sold the portrait to Duarte. However, if this were the case, given the historical and artistic significance of the piece, the National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL) would have been required to receive notification. Another version indicates that the painting remains in the possession of Gabriel’s family, in one of their properties in New York or Las Vegas.

Be that as it may, the piece is still missing. Perhaps the fact that María Félix did not want it displayed cast a spell over Diego Rivera’s portrait of her — never to be seen again, not by her, not by anyone.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Mexico has a trash-dumping problem. Could this new clean-up project from Monterrey be the fix?
World.content:
You see it across Mexico — on roadways, over vacant lots and along waterways. But a new project aims to create a model that could help cities tackle the nation’s illegal trash-dumping problem.

In the northern state of Nuevo León, a Tecnológico de Monterrey project is testing whether data, cleanup campaigns and community participation can turn one trash-strewn stream into a model for urban restoration.

The Arroyo Vivo initiative focuses on the 13-kilometer Arroyo Seco-San Agustín, a waterway where several sections have become illegal dumping grounds. The stream begins in the mountains above Monterrey and flows through the city before joining the La Silla River.

During 16 cleanup days since the project launched in late 2022, Tec de Monterrey researchers and volunteers have removed 21 tons of waste, finding that plastics made up more than 70% of the debris. Textiles, tires and construction rubble were also common.

The project plans to use algorithms to analyze street-level images and photographs submitted by residents, helping identify and estimate the volume of waste along the stream.

It also aims to create a biological corridor along the waterway, benefiting wildlife and nearby residents. Restoring the stream could also reduce pollution and help limit flooding risks in communities along its route during heavy rains.

Researchers are developing three-, five- and 10-year plans, while acknowledging that full ecosystem restoration could take decades.

“It’s a platform with a long-term vision,” said Nélida Escobedo, a Tec researcher. “We’re looking to consolidate a replicable intervention model that will trigger a process of ecological, social and urban regeneration in Arroyo Seco.”

The problem, of course, reaches far beyond Monterrey. Mexico City officials identified 889 illegal dumps in February, nearly half in the Cuauhtémoc, Iztapalapa and Miguel Hidalgo boroughs.

Nationally, 21% of municipal solid waste was deposited at uncontrolled sites in 2012, according to a 2015 environmental report by Semarnat, Mexico’s Environment Ministry.

The report found that 90% of metropolitan areas used sanitary landfills or controlled disposal sites, but only 4.5% of rural and semi-urban localities used sanitary landfills or controlled disposal sites.

An earlier Semarnat report, using 2011 data, put the rural and semi-urban figure at 13%.

With reports from TecScience and La Jornada

World.title: Where to Eat Chile en Nogada in Querétaro This 2026 Season
World.content:
Mexico · Food

Key Facts — The dish A roasted poblano stuffed with pork-and-fruit picadillo, draped in walnut cream and scattered with pomegranate seeds.

— The season It runs from roughly July through Wednesday, 30 September 2026, tied to the fresh walnut and pomegranate harvest.

— The price Plates in Querétaro run from about 374 MXN (US$22) up to around 490 MXN (US$29) this year.

— Where La Parrilla Leonesa (Constituyentes 138 and Bernardo Quintana 536) and Cócono at Bernardo Quintana 18 both serve it in season.

— How Reserve ahead, especially near Independence Day on Wednesday, 16 September 2026, when tables fill fast.

The green-white-red plate returns to Querétaro tables only from summer to late September, and here is where you can actually find it.

Chile en nogada shown with its ingredients: the seasonal poblano dish in the colors of the Mexican flag, served in Querétaro from summer to late September. (Photo: German Abal, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
