Chile en nogada is the one dish that tells you Mexico’s patriotic season has arrived. And in Querétaro it appears for only a few short weeks.

This roasted poblano, cloaked in cool walnut cream and jeweled with pomegranate, shows up on menus from summer until late September. So if you want to try it this year, the clock is already running.

For expats settling into the city, it is one of the most rewarding seasonal traditions to catch.

What chile en nogada actually is

At heart it is a roasted, peeled poblano chile stuffed with picadillo. That filling mixes pork with apple, pear, peach, dried fruit and nuts.

The chile is then covered in nogada, a cold cream sauce made from fresh Castilla walnuts. Finally, pomegranate seeds and parsley go on top.

The taste is famously sweet and savory at once, which surprises many first-timers. So do not expect a spicy plate, because the poblano here is mild.

A dish with a patriotic backstory

The recipe is tied to the city of Puebla and to Mexican Independence. By tradition, nuns are said to have created it to honor the Trigarante Army.

That history is why the plate turns up every patriotic season. Because of it, ordering chile en nogada in September feels like joining a national ritual.

A plate that flies the Mexican flag

The colors are the whole point, so nothing here is accidental. Green comes from the chile and parsley, white from the walnut sauce, red from the pomegranate.

Together they mirror the Mexican flag, which is why the dish belongs to Independence season. It is usually served at room temperature, because the nogada is meant to stay cool.

Why the season is so short

The timing is not marketing, but agriculture. Fresh Castilla walnuts and ripe pomegranates are only around in late summer, so the dish follows the harvest.

As a result, most Querétaro kitchens serve it from about July through late September. After Independence Day on Wednesday, 16 September 2026, the window starts to close.

La Parrilla Leonesa, the easy first stop

This local steakhouse group runs its chile en nogada season across both branches. You will find it at Constituyentes 138 and at Bernardo Quintana 536.

For 2026 the restaurant has advertised the plate from July until Wednesday, 30 September 2026. Because it is a limited-time special, it is worth calling before you go.

Cócono Gusto Mexicano, the local favorite

Cócono, at Bernardo Quintana 18 in Colonia La Calesa, has built a reputation on this one dish. In fact, it has run a dedicated chile en nogada season for years.

Diners regularly single it out as some of the best in the city. Still, it only appears in season, so a mid-week visit is the safest bet.

What a plate will cost you

Expect a premium, since this is a labor-heavy seasonal dish. La Parrilla Leonesa has promoted its version at about 374 MXN, roughly US$22.

Elsewhere in Querétaro, single plates cluster near 380 to 395 MXN, about US$22 to US$23. Larger portions can reach around 490 MXN, close to US$29, at roughly 17.03 pesos to the dollar.

That may sound steep for a single chile, yet the portion is large and rich. Because the walnuts are fresh and hand-peeled, the price reflects real seasonal work.

How to book and when to go

Reserving ahead matters more than usual during this season. Because demand peaks around the patriotic holidays, weekend tables can vanish quickly.

The safest plan is a weekday lunch earlier in the run. Independence Day itself, Wednesday, 16 September 2026, is the busiest date of all.

Getting there and finding it

Both restaurants sit along the Bernardo Quintana and Constituyentes corridors, easy to reach by taxi or app ride. So you will not need a car of your own.

If a menu does not list the dish, just ask, since some kitchens run it as a daily special. Many other Querétaro restaurants also add it during the mes patrio.

Tips before the window closes

First, do not wait, because the best kitchens sell out as September ends. The season effectively finishes on Wednesday, 30 September 2026.

Second, order it the traditional way rather than battered, if you have a choice. Finally, bring an appetite, since one plate is genuinely a full meal.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is chile en nogada available in Querétaro?

It runs from roughly July through late September 2026, peaking around Independence Day. Most kitchens stop serving it after Wednesday, 30 September 2026.

How much does chile en nogada cost?

In Querétaro, plates run from about 374 MXN (US$22) to around 490 MXN (US$29). Prices depend on the restaurant and portion size.

Where can I eat it in Querétaro?

La Parrilla Leonesa serves it at Constituyentes 138 and Bernardo Quintana 536. Cócono Gusto Mexicano offers it at Bernardo Quintana 18.

Do I need a reservation?

It helps a lot, especially on weekends and around 16 September. A weekday lunch earlier in the season is the easiest way in.

Sources: Queretaro.travel; Queretanízate; local restaurant listings; Banco de México (FX).

World.title: Panama vs Costa Rica: Is Panama the New Costa Rica for Retirees in 2026?
World.content:
Expats · Comparison

Key Facts — Panama Pensionado US$1,000/month lifetime pension, or US$750 if you buy a US$100,000 home; add US$250 per dependent

— Costa Rica options Pensionado US$1,000/month pension; Rentista US$2,500/month or a US$60,000 deposit; Inversionista from US$150,000

— Taxes both run territorial systems, so foreign pensions and overseas investment income are not taxed in either country

— Monthly budget a couple lives comfortably on about US$2,500-3,500 in Panama City, or US$2,000-3,500 in Costa Rica’s Central Valley

— Getting around Panama City runs a two-line metro and the Tocumen (PTY) hub; Costa Rica flies mainly through San Jose (SJO)

Costa Rica has long been the poster child for tropical retirement. But a dollar economy, a metro and a famously easy retiree visa are turning heads north.

Panama City’s dense wall of high-rise towers, a key draw for retirees weighing it against Costa Rica. Illustrative photo. (Photo: Guillaume Baviere, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

If you are weighing Panama vs Costa Rica for your retirement, you are really choosing between two different daily lives. Both let you keep your foreign pension tax-free and both welcome retirees with open arms.

Yet one gives you a dollar-priced, high-rise city, while the other offers rainforest, surf and a slower pace.

Two Very Different Tropical Lives

Costa Rica built its name on nature. Think national parks, volcanoes, empty beaches and the easy pura vida attitude that greets you everywhere.

Panama sells something else entirely. Its capital is a wall of glass towers, air-conditioned malls and a working metro, all priced in US dollars.

So the honest question is not which country is better. It is which version of tropical living actually fits how you want to spend your days.

Residency: The Two Pensionado Visas Compared

Panama’s Pensionado is the star of the show. You qualify with a lifetime pension of just US$1,000 a month, and it grants permanent residency almost straight away.

That figure drops to US$750 a month if you buy a home worth at least US$100,000. A couple simply adds US$250 for the dependent spouse.

Costa Rica’s Pensionado also asks for a guaranteed lifetime pension of US$1,000 a month. Because it is a fixed benefit, ordinary savings or dividends usually will not count.

If you lack a formal pension, Costa Rica still has doors open. The Rentista route needs US$2,500 a month in passive income, or a US$60,000 bank deposit drawn down over two years.

Investors get a third path. The Inversionista visa starts at a US$150,000 investment, often in property held in your own name.

How the Taxman Treats You

Here the two countries are twins. Both use a territorial tax system, which means only money earned inside the country is taxed.

As a result, your US Social Security, foreign pension and overseas investment income are not taxed in either Panama or Costa Rica. In Panama, local income is also gentle, with the first US$11,000 taxed at zero.

For most retirees living on foreign income, the effective income-tax bill is simply nothing.

What It Costs to Live

Day to day, the two are closer than you might expect. A couple can live comfortably on roughly US$2,500-3,500 a month in Panama City.

Costa Rica’s Central Valley towns, such as Atenas or Grecia, run a touch lower at about US$2,000-3,500 for a couple. Rent is where the gap widens.

A central one-bedroom in Panama City tends to cost US$900-1,400 a month. In a mid-range Costa Rican town, however, the same apartment often runs just US$400-800.

Popular beach spots in Guanacaste, by contrast, can cost far more.

Buying Property in Either Country

Foreigners can own property outright in both countries, with the same title rights as locals. That security is a big reason expats feel comfortable buying.

In Panama City, mid-range apartments are often quoted around US$1,800-2,500 per square meter, with waterfront towers well above that. Costa Rica’s Central Valley is broadly similar at roughly US$1,500-2,500 per square meter.

Prime beach areas naturally climb higher. One caveat before you fall for a beach: Costa Rica restricts building in the first 200 meters of shoreline.

Known as the maritime zone.

Healthcare: Caja vs Pensionado Discounts

Costa Rica folds you into its public system, the Caja. Legal residents must enroll and pay a monthly fee based on income, usually around 5% to 11%.

That fee, as little as roughly US$52 a month on a US$1,000 pension, buys unlimited public care for you and your spouse. Panama leans the other way, toward private hospitals paired with generous pensionado discounts.

Retirees get 20% off medical consultations and 20% off prescription medicines. Many expat couples in Panama City still carry private insurance, typically budgeting US$300-500 a month.

Both countries offer respected private hospitals with English-speaking, often US-trained doctors.

The Pensionado Perks That Set Panama Apart

Panama’s discount law is unusually broad, and it applies from the day you get residency. These perks are written into the country’s Law 6.

You get 25% off sit-down restaurant meals and 25% off airline tickets. Hotels are 50% off from Monday to Thursday.

Utilities join the party too, with 25% off electricity up to 600 kWh a month. Movies and cultural events are half price as well.

Costa Rica has no equivalent nationwide discount card. Instead, its value comes from cheaper rents and that all-in Caja health cover.

City Comforts vs Getting Around

Panama City feels like a small Miami on the isthmus. It has a two-line metro plus an airport spur, reliable utilities and fast internet.

Its Tocumen airport (PTY) is a major regional hub, so flights home are frequent and often cheap. A third metro line is under construction.

Costa Rica is more spread out and more rural once you leave the capital. Coastal roads can be slow, and most flights route through San Jose (SJO).

For pure convenience, therefore, Panama City wins. For waking up to birdsong and forest, Costa Rica is hard to beat.

Panama vs Costa Rica: Who Should Choose Which

Choose Panama if you want a modern, walkable city, a dollar economy and the easiest retiree visa in the region. It suits convenience-seekers and property investors.

Choose Costa Rica if nature is the whole point. Beaches, mountains, biodiversity and a slower rhythm reward those happy to trade some polish for peace.

In short, the Panama vs Costa Rica choice comes down to city polish against wild green calm. Panama is the new Costa Rica for city lovers, yet the original still owns laid-back living.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Panama or Costa Rica cheaper for retirees?

Costa Rica’s inland towns usually win on rent, with one-bedrooms from US$400-800. Panama City costs more to rent but pays it back through pensionado discounts.

How much pension do I need for each retiree visa?

Both Pensionado visas require a US$1,000 a month lifetime pension. Panama drops that to US$750 if you buy a US$100,000 home.

Do I pay tax on my foreign pension in either country?

No. Both Panama and Costa Rica use territorial tax systems, so foreign pensions and overseas investment income are not taxed.

Can foreigners own property in Panama and Costa Rica?

Yes, in both. Foreigners hold full title with the same rights as locals, though Costa Rica limits building in the first 200 meters of shoreline.

Sources: Panama and Costa Rica immigration and tax guidance, expat relocation reports, and Panama Metro / Tocumen airport information, verified August 2026.

World.title: Living in Ciudad Quesada: A 2026 Guide for Expats in Costa Rica
World.content:
Costa Rica · Living

Key Facts — Getting there About 90 km from San José, roughly an hour and a half to two hours by car via Route 141 through Naranjo and Zarcero.

— Rent A one-bedroom runs about ₡85,000 to ₡220,000 (US$190 to US$490); a two-bedroom typically US$500 to US$700.

— Healthcare Public care through the CCSS (la Caja) at Hospital de San Carlos; a private option, Hospital San Carlos Borromeo, sits in town.

— Residency Pensionado needs US$1,000 a month; rentista US$2,500 a month for two years, or a US$60,000 deposit; investor US$150,000.

— Climate Northern highlands at about 650 metres, cooler and wetter than the coast, roughly 22°C to 26°C most of the year.

A cool, green working town in Costa Rica’s dairy country. San Carlos trades beach glamour for lower rents, solid public healthcare and an unhurried daily pace.

Living in Ciudad Quesada: A 2026 Guide for Expats in Costa Rica. (Photo internet reproduction)

Ciudad Quesada is the kind of Costa Rica town that rarely makes the postcards, and that is exactly its charm. Sitting in the green northern highlands, it is the busy capital of the San Carlos canton in Alajuela province.

Instead of beach resorts you get dairy farms, a working market town and a noticeably lower cost of living. If you want the real country rather than the brochure, it deserves a close look.

Getting to Ciudad Quesada from San José

Start with the drive, because most newcomers land at San José’s airport first. Ciudad Quesada sits about 90 kilometres north of the capital.

By car the trip takes roughly an hour and a half to two hours, depending on traffic and weather. The usual route follows Route 141, climbing through Naranjo and the flower town of Zarcero.

That climb is scenic but winding, so take it slowly if you are new to Costa Rican roads. Regular buses also run the corridor, which helps if you would rather not own a car at first.

The setting and the climate

The town sits at about 650 metres above sea level, high enough to shake off the coastal heat. Temperatures generally sit between 22°C and 26°C (roughly 72°F to 79°F) all year.

In return for that comfort, you accept rain. This is one of the wetter parts of the country, with annual rainfall around 3,271 millimetres.

So expect green hills, afternoon downpours and cool evenings rather than tropical beach weather. Many people find the mild highland climate far easier to live in day to day.

What it costs to rent

Housing is where San Carlos really rewards you. A one-bedroom apartment ranges from about ₡85,000 (US$190) outside the centre to around ₡220,000 (US$490) in town.

A two-bedroom apartment or small house typically lands in the US$500 to US$700 range. For more space, a three-bedroom outside the centre runs near ₡300,000 (US$665).

Prices vary with furnishing, condition and how close you are to the plaza. Because listings move by word of mouth, it pays to visit, ask around and rent short-term before you commit.

Groceries, utilities and everyday spending

Day-to-day costs stay reasonable if you shop like a local. For a couple, groceries usually come to about US$450 to US$600 a month, especially if you use the weekly farmers’ market.

Utilities are gentle in the highlands, since you rarely need air conditioning. Electricity and water together often run US$40 to US$80, and home internet is another US$30 to US$50.

Imported goods and restaurant meals cost more, as they do everywhere in Costa Rica. Still, a modest, mostly local lifestyle here stretches a pension or remote salary comfortably.

Healthcare and the Caja

Costa Rica’s public health system is the CCSS, known to everyone simply as la Caja. Once you hold residency, you enroll and pay a monthly contribution based on your declared income.

As a rough guide, that works out to somewhere around 7% to 11% of income. For a retired couple that often means about US$150 to US$250 a month, though the Caja calculates each case individually.

The main public hospital for the region is Hospital de San Carlos, right in Ciudad Quesada. Because it is a regional hospital, it handles far more than a small-town clinic would.

Private clinics and specialist care

Plenty of residents mix public and private care, paying out of pocket for speed. In town, Hospital San Carlos Borromeo offers a private option close to home.

For complex procedures or a second opinion, many people drive to Greater San José. There you find the big private hospitals: CIMA in Escazú, Clínica Bíblica and Hospital Metropolitano.

That trip is the trade-off for choosing a quieter town. Even so, everyday medical needs are well covered without ever leaving San Carlos.

Visas and residency basics

Most expats settle in under one of three residency categories. The pensionado route is for retirees and requires a lifetime pension of at least US$1,000 a month.

The rentista option suits those with steady income but no pension. It asks you to show US$2,500 a month for two years, or to place a US$60,000 deposit with a Costa Rican bank.

If you plan to invest, the inversionista route currently sets the bar at US$150,000. In every case, use a local attorney, since the paperwork and timelines change.

The expat community and daily life

Ciudad Quesada is not a packed expat enclave like some beach towns, and that suits many people. There is an established foreign community here, but it stays small and low-key.

As a result, daily life feels genuinely Costa Rican rather than staged for outsiders. You will pick up more Spanish, meet more neighbours and spend far less than in the tourist zones.

The town has supermarkets, banks, a hospital, schools and a lively central market. Meanwhile, the surrounding San Carlos countryside offers hot springs, waterfalls and the road toward La Fortuna and Arenal.

Is Ciudad Quesada right for you?

Be honest with yourself about the rain and the quiet before you move. If you crave nightlife, beaches and a large English-speaking crowd, this may not be your town.

But if you want a cooler climate, low costs and a real community, it delivers. In short, Ciudad Quesada rewards people who value everyday life over a permanent holiday.

The smart approach is to rent for a few months first and test the fit. That way you learn the roads, the weather and the rhythm before signing anything long-term.

Frequently Asked Questions

How far is Ciudad Quesada from San José?

It is about 90 kilometres north of San José. Driving takes roughly an hour and a half to two hours via Route 141 through Naranjo and Zarcero.

How much does it cost to live there?

Rent runs from about US$190 to US$490 for a one-bedroom, and US$500 to US$700 for a two-bedroom. Groceries for a couple are roughly US$450 to US$600 a month.

What are the residency requirements?

The pensionado route needs a US$1,000 monthly pension. The rentista route needs US$2,500 a month for two years or a US$60,000 deposit, and the investor route needs US$150,000.

Is the healthcare good?

Yes. Residents use the public CCSS, or Caja, at Hospital de San Carlos.

Sources: Numbeo; CityCost; XE; Costa Rica Board; Wikipedia list of hospitals in Costa Rica; UK Government list of medical facilities in Costa Rica.

World.title: AES Andes Completes US$1.3 Billion Solar-Storage Hub in Chile
World.content:
Chile · Energy

Key Facts — The hub The Andes Solar Hub in Chile’s Antofagasta region now holds 692 MW of solar panels and 510 MW of battery storage.

— The milestone Its final piece, Andes Solar III, began commercial operation on April 14, 2026.

— The money AES Andes says total investment in the hub topped US$1.3 billion over almost a decade.

— The batteries Andes Solar III alone added a 171 MW battery system that can discharge for about three hours.

— The coal link AES Andes shut its Norgener coal plant in April 2024, part of Chile’s plan to leave coal by 2040.

The complex pairs daytime solar with big batteries, letting the grid lean on sunshine long after the sun goes down.

Illustrative photo: solar panels at the La Silla site in Chile. AES Andes says its Andes Solar Hub now pairs 692 MW of solar with 510 MW of battery storage. (Photo: EGP/ESO, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

AES Andes, the Chilean arm of US power group AES, has finished a sprawling solar-and-battery complex in the northern desert. The Andes Solar Hub now bundles 692 MW of solar panels with 510 MW of battery storage.

The company calls it the largest project of its kind in Latin America.

What AES Andes just switched on

The final building block, called Andes Solar III, started commercial operation on April 14, 2026. Notably, it sits in the Antofagasta region, in one of the sunniest deserts on Earth.

As a result, the whole hub reached 692 MW of solar capacity and 510 MW of batteries. Meanwhile, AES Andes puts the total spend at more than US$1.3 billion.

Why the batteries matter more than the panels

Solar panels only work while the sun is up. However, that is a problem in the evening, when homes and factories still need power.

The batteries fix the timing. Specifically, they soak up cheap midday sunshine and release it after dark.

So the grid can rely on solar for far more hours.

A closer look at Andes Solar III

The newest plant is more than panels. It carries a 171 MW battery system that can pump out power for about three hours.

In short, that kind of storage turns a daytime-only source into something the grid can plan around. It is the difference between a nice extra and a real workhorse.

How the hub grew over a decade

The complex was not built overnight. Instead, AES Andes assembled it in stages over nearly ten years, adding capacity piece by piece.

An earlier phase, Andes Solar IV, came online in October 2024 near Calama, about 230 km east of Antofagasta. It brought a large 130 MW battery able to run for five hours.

Where the project sits in Chile

Northern Chile is prime solar territory. The Atacama Desert gets some of the strongest, steadiest sunlight anywhere on the planet.

That geography is why so many solar plants cluster there. The hard part has always been storing the power and moving it to where people live.

AES Andes and the retreat from coal

The company is not only adding clean power. It is also unplugging its old coal units under a strategy it brands Greentegra.

AES Andes disconnected its Norgener coal plant in the north in April 2024, well ahead of an earlier 2025 target. More coal units are lined up to close.

Chile’s wider coal phase-out

Chile set out in 2019 to close every coal-fired plant by 2040 and reach carbon neutrality by 2050. Officials have floated pulling that date forward.

The government also aimed to retire a big share of coal capacity by 2025. Projects like this hub are meant to fill the gap coal leaves behind.

How big is ‘the largest in Latin America’?

AES Andes describes the hub as the region’s largest solar-plus-storage complex. That claim comes from the company itself, not an independent ranking.

Even so, the scale is real. A combined 692 MW of solar and 510 MW of batteries on one site is unusual anywhere, let alone in one desert.

What it means for the grid and for customers

More stored solar means fewer hours when the system has to burn gas or coal to keep the lights on. That tends to steady both emissions and costs.

It also gives big industrial buyers a cleaner supply. Mining, which dominates northern Chile, is under growing pressure to cut its carbon footprint.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Andes Solar Hub?

It is a solar-and-battery complex built by AES Andes in Chile’s Antofagasta region. It now holds 692 MW of solar capacity and 510 MW of battery storage.

How much did AES Andes spend on it?

AES Andes says total investment in the hub exceeded US$1.3 billion, spread across nearly a decade of construction in stages.

Why are the batteries important?

Solar panels only produce power in daylight. The batteries store midday energy and release it after sunset, so the grid can depend on solar for more of the day.

How does this connect to coal?

AES Andes is retiring its coal plants, including Norgener in 2024, under Chile’s plan to leave coal by 2040. New solar and storage help replace that lost capacity.

Sources: AES Chile; AES Andes; SoyChile; PV Magazine.

World.title: Pixbet Accused of Using Tax IDs of 549 Dead People, Federal Police Say
World.content:
Brazil · Justice

Key Facts — The operation Federal Police launched Operacao Arena on August 13, 2026, targeting a betting group centered on Pixbet.

— The allegation Investigators say 549 tax IDs of deceased people were used to create false identities for illegal currency operations.

— The money trail A court authorized freezing up to R$1.1 billion (about US$212 million) in assets linked to the group.

— The scale Tax authorities flagged more than R$2 billion (about US$385 million) in suspicious transactions between 2022 and 2025.

— The response Pixbet’s defense said it was caught by surprise and had not yet seen the court order.

A federal court has authorized freezing up to R$1.1 billion (about US$212 million) in assets tied to the betting group.

Illustrative photo: Brazilian Federal Police agents during an operation. In the Pixbet case, police say 549 dead people’s tax IDs were used in illegal currency deals. (Photo: Rovena Rosa, CC BY 3.0 br, Wikimedia Commons.)

Pixbet, one of Brazil’s biggest betting brands. Stands accused of using the tax IDs of 549 dead people to disguise illegal money transfers abroad.

Federal Police made the claim as they raided the company across several states on August 13, 2026. Some of those tax IDs belonged to people who had died more than 20 years earlier.

What the Federal Police say Pixbet did

Investigators say the numbers, known in Brazil as CPFs, were slipped into paperwork for foreign-exchange deals. As a result, each dead person’s ID became a fake identity on transactions that moved money out of the country.

Police call this evasao de divisas, or the illegal export of currency. Moreover, they say it was paired with money laundering that routed funds to a tax haven.

The 549 dead people at the center of the case

The figure of 549 tax IDs comes straight from Federal Police documents, as reported by Brazil’s largest news outlets. For example, officers found the numbers scattered through financial records tied to the betting group.

What unsettled investigators is how old some of the records were. In several cases, the person whose ID was used had been dead for more than two decades.

Although the paperwork made them look active.

Operation Arena and the raids

The case is called Operacao Arena, and it went public on Thursday, August 13, 2026. Meanwhile, police carried out search-and-seizure orders in Paraiba, Sao Paulo and other states.

The betting group is headquartered in Paraiba, a northeastern state that has. In fact, become an unlikely hub for Brazil’s online gambling industry.

How Pixbet is said to have moved the money

Prosecutors describe a scheme built to hide where the cash came from and where it went. For instance, betting revenue was allegedly funneled through companies abroad and into cryptocurrency.

Much of the money, meanwhile, allegedly flowed to Curacao. A Caribbean island widely used as a tax haven and a base for offshore gambling firms.

The billion-real question about assets

A federal court in Paraiba authorized the freezing of up to R$1.1 billion. Or roughly US$212 million, in assets connected to those under investigation.

The order covers property and financial holdings. It is one of the largest asset freezes yet in a Brazilian betting case.

The size hints at how much money regulators believe passed through the network.

Two billion reais in suspicious flows

Brazil’s tax authority, the Receita Federal, said it spotted more than R$2 billion, about US$385 million, in suspicious transactions. Those movements span the years 2022 to 2025.

That figure sits above the frozen assets and captures the wider flow of cash, not just what officials could seize.

The license and the lingering doubts

Pixbet paid R$30 million, close to US$5.8 million, for its federal betting license in late 2024. It won national authorization to operate early the following year.

Still, tax officials have questioned whether that license fee itself was paid with illicit money. That suspicion is now part of the broader investigation.

Was Pixbet a victim or a player?

Police were careful about one point. They say there are signs the company was not simply a victim of identity theft.

But an active part of the fraudulent paperwork. Still, how the data of dead people was obtained remains unclear, investigators admit.

That thread is being pulled even so.

The government moves in parallel

On the same day as the raids, Brazil’s Finance Ministry suspended Pixbet’s license and barred it from taking new bets. Officials framed this as an administrative step, separate from the criminal case.

The company can honor bets already placed but cannot sign up fresh wagers while the suspension holds.

How Pixbet has responded

Pixbet’s defense said the company was caught by surprise and had not been given access to the order that authorized the operation. It has not issued a detailed rebuttal of the money-laundering claims.

In an earlier regulatory clash this year. The company stressed what it called an uncompromising commitment to legality and to following the rules.

A full answer to the criminal allegations has yet to come.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Pixbet accused of?

Federal Police say Pixbet used the tax IDs of 549 deceased people to create false identities for unauthorized foreign-exchange deals. Part of an alleged scheme of illegal currency export and money laundering.

What is Operation Arena?

It is the Federal Police operation, launched on August 13, 2026. That targeted the betting group centered on Pixbet with raids across several Brazilian states.

How much money is involved?

A court authorized freezing up to R$1.1 billion (about US$212 million) in assets. And tax authorities flagged more than R$2 billion (about US$385 million) in suspicious transactions from 2022 to 2025.

Can people still bet on Pixbet?

No. Brazil’s Finance Ministry suspended the company’s license and barred it from accepting new bets. Though bets already placed can still be honored.

Sources: G1 (Globo); Veja; Folha de S.Paulo; Estadao; Poder360.

World.title: Guatemala Tourism Draws 1.6 Million Visitors in First Half of 2026
World.content:
Guatemala · Tourism

Key Facts — The count Guatemala logged 1,625,849 non-resident visitors between January and June 2026, up about 1% on a year earlier.

— The gain That was 14,944 more arrivals than the same six months of 2025, a modest but steady rise.

— The money Tourism generated US$1,390.2 million in foreign exchange for Guatemala in 2025, an official record.

— The 2026 pace Visitor spending reached US$523 million from January to May 2026, up 0.86% year over year.

— The target INGUAT wants 3.63 million arrivals and US$1.516 billion in receipts this year, aiming for 4 million by 2027.

The sector earned Guatemala US$1.39 billion last year, and the government is now chasing 3.63 million arrivals in 2026.

Guatemala tourism kept climbing through the first half of 2026, with 1,625,849 non-resident visitors arriving between January and June. That was roughly 14,944 more than the same stretch of 2025, a gain of about 1%.

The country’s tourism board wants far bigger numbers before the year ends.

What the first-half numbers show

The figures come from INGUAT, Guatemala’s national tourism institute. In its July report, the agency counted 1,625,849 non-resident visitors for the first six months of the year.

That is a small increase over 2025, not a boom. Still, it keeps Guatemala on an upward path after a strong prior year.

Why Guatemala tourism matters to the economy

Tourism is one of the few sectors that brings fresh foreign money straight into the country. Visitors pay in dollars for hotels, meals, guides, transport and handicrafts.

That hard currency helps Guatemala pay for imports and steady its finances. It also spreads income to small towns, where jobs are otherwise scarce.

The money tourists leave behind

In 2025, tourism generated US$1,390.2 million in foreign exchange, an official record for Guatemala. For a mid-sized economy, that is a meaningful stream of dollars.

The pace has held up in 2026. Between January and May, visitor spending reached US$523 million, a rise of 0.86% from a year earlier.

Where the visitors come from

Most arrivals are regional. Central America supplied the bulk of visitors, and El Salvador and the United States remain the two largest single-country markets.

That mix matters because nearby travelers are easy to attract and quick to return. However, both El Salvador and the US dipped slightly in the first half of 2026.

New markets are picking up the slack

The overall gain came from further afield. In the first half, arrivals from Colombia jumped about 42%, from Japan around 39%, and from Russia roughly 30%.

As a result, Guatemala offset softer demand from its two biggest markets. That broader spread makes the sector less dependent on any single country.

A record 2025 set a high bar

Guatemala closed 2025 with 3,361,843 non-resident visitors. That was up 11% from 3,037,282 the year before, a strong jump.

Because 2025 was so busy, matching it in 2026 was always going to be hard. In that light, the modest first-half growth still counts as progress.

The government’s ambitious 2026 target

INGUAT is aiming high for the full year. It wants 3.63 million arrivals and about US$1.516 billion in tourism receipts by December.

The longer goal is bolder still. Officials are targeting 4 million visitors by 2027, backed by promotion abroad and a push on sustainable travel.

What could slow things down

Reaching those numbers will not be easy. With growth running near 1% so far, the second half would need to accelerate sharply.

Softer demand from El Salvador and the US is the main risk. Yet rising interest from South America, Asia and Europe offers a way to close the gap.

What to watch next

The next INGUAT bulletins will show whether the far-flung markets keep surging. They will also reveal if regional travel recovers in the busy year-end season.

For now, Guatemala tourism is growing, if slowly. The bigger question is whether promotion can turn that steady trickle into the surge the government wants.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many tourists visited Guatemala in early 2026?

Guatemala received 1,625,849 non-resident visitors between January and June 2026, about 1% more than the same period of 2025.

How much does tourism earn Guatemala?

Tourism generated US$1,390.2 million in foreign exchange in 2025. From January to May 2026, spending reached US$523 million.

Where do most visitors to Guatemala come from?

Most come from Central America, with El Salvador and the United States as the biggest single-country markets. Colombia, Japan and Russia grew fast in 2026.

What are Guatemala’s tourism goals?

INGUAT is targeting 3.63 million arrivals and about US$1.516 billion in receipts in 2026. With a longer-term goal of 4 million visitors by 2027.

Sources: INGUAT; Banguat; Prensa Libre.

World.title: Affiliation Fraud at Brazil’s TSE Ensnares Lula and Bolsonaro
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — The scheme Forged sign-ups use a real person’s name, CPF and voter ID to log party memberships they never requested.

— The Lula case A fake 2023 sign-up listed the president in the rival PL, briefly erasing him from his own Workers’ Party.

— The 2026 twist In August someone tried to enroll Lula in the small Democracia Cristã party; its leaders blocked it first.

— The Bolsonaro hit Flávio Bolsonaro was switched from the PL to a party called Missão overnight on August 12, without consent.

— The response TSE chief Kassio Nunes Marques suspended new affiliation processing on August 13, 2026, and called in federal police.

A string of forged party sign-ups forced the electoral court to freeze new memberships days before the candidate deadline.

The Tribunal Superior Eleitoral headquarters in Brasília. The TSE suspended new affiliation processing on August 13, 2026, after fraud hit Lula’s and Flávio Bolsonaro’s records. (Photo: O Tribunal da Democracia, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.)

Affiliation fraud has widened into a serious problem at Brazil’s top electoral court, the TSE. Forged party sign-ups have already dragged in President Lula and senator Flávio Bolsonaro, forcing the court to freeze new memberships.

The tricks are simple, and the damage is real.

A quiet scam surfaces at the electoral court

For years, Brazilians could join a party through a simple online form. You typed your name, your CPF tax number and your voter ID, and the request flowed to the electoral court.

That convenience became a weapon. Fraudsters started filing sign-ups in other people’s names, and the fakes landed in official records before anyone noticed.

What affiliation fraud actually means

Affiliation fraud happens when someone is registered in a party without their knowledge or consent. The forger uses real personal data to make the request look genuine.

Because the court trusts the parties that submit these forms, a single false entry can quietly rewrite a citizen’s political record. In Brazil, that is treated as a crime of ideological falsehood.

How Lula was pulled out of his own party

The clearest example began in July 2023. The court’s system suddenly showed President Lula as a member of the rival Liberal Party, or PL.

Since the newest membership overrides the older one. The fake entry marked Lula as detached from the Workers’ Party from July 15, 2023.

He had belonged to the PT since 1981.

A cancelled password and a police case

Investigators found no hacking. Instead, the false entry was made using the valid login of a PL lawyer.

Ana Daniela Leite e Aguiar, whose password was then cancelled. The court reversed the change and restored Lula to the PT.

Then justice Alexandre de Moraes sent the case to the Federal Police, which opened Operação Infiliatio on October 30, 2024.

The 2026 attempt to move Lula again

The problem returned this month. In August 2026, someone posing as Lula filled out a sign-up for the small Democracia Cristã party using his real data.

Including his RG and CPF. This time the party caught it first.

Its president, João Caldas, said the executive spotted the fraud and blocked the form before it ever reached the electoral court.

Flávio Bolsonaro caught in the same trap

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro was hit almost at the same time. Overnight on August 12, his record was switched from the PL to a newly created party called Missão, without his consent.

The change automatically detached him from the PL and blocked his presidential candidacy. Both Bolsonaro’s camp and Missão say they were victims of the forgery.

Why one fake sign-up erases the old party

The mischief works because of a simple rule. Under Brazil’s party law, when two memberships overlap, the most recent one prevails and the others are cancelled automatically.

So a forged sign-up does not just add a fake party. It silently deletes the real one, unless the court steps in to undo the damage.

The TSE freezes new memberships

The court moved fast once the pattern was clear. On August 13, 2026, TSE president Kassio Nunes Marques restored Bolsonaro to the PL and ordered the Missão entry deleted.

He also suspended the processing of new party sign-ups and preserved the system’s access logs. The freeze arrived just before the August 15 deadline for registering candidates.

What it means for the October vote

The timing is delicate. Brazil votes in October 2026, and a wrong party label can knock a candidate off the ballot or upend a campaign.

For ordinary voters, the lesson is plainer still. Many people only learn they were signed up elsewhere when they check their own status online.

Background: Brazil Tax Reform Timeline: Tech Sector Faces 2026 Invoice Shock.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is affiliation fraud in Brazil?

It is the registration of a person in a political party without their consent, using their real name, CPF and voter ID. Brazilian law treats it as ideological falsehood.

Was Lula really removed from the Workers’ Party?

Yes, briefly. A fake 2023 sign-up listed him in the PL, which automatically detached him from the PT until the court reversed it.

What happened to Flávio Bolsonaro?

His record was switched from the PL to a party called Missão overnight on August 12, 2026, without his consent. The TSE restored his PL membership the next day.

How did the TSE respond?

President Kassio Nunes Marques suspended the processing of new party sign-ups on August 13. 2026, preserved system logs, and referred the cases to the Federal Police.

Sources: Polícia Federal; Tribunal Superior Eleitoral; CNN Brasil; UOL.

World.title: El Salvador and Belize Sign Partial-Scope Trade Deal Covering 400 Tariff Lines
World.content:
El Salvador · Trade

Key Facts — The deal El Salvador and Belize agreed a Partial Scope Agreement covering around 400 tariff lines of goods, reported in mid-August 2026.

— The signers El Salvador’s Economy Minister Maria Luisa Hayem and Belize’s Minister of State for Foreign Trade Marconi Leal signed the accord.

— The scope It grants preferential access and cuts non-tariff barriers, but it is a partial-scope pact, not a comprehensive free-trade agreement.

— The goods Highlighted sectors include agro-industry, pharmaceuticals, plastics, textiles and metalworking.

— The path Talks began with a 2023 framework, a first round in Belmopan in December 2024, and technical negotiations wrapped up in October 2024.

The accord is a targeted goods deal, not a full free-trade agreement. And both governments still must ratify it before it takes effect.

Illustrative photo: the container park at Barbados Port in Bridgetown. El Salvador and Belize signed a Partial Scope Agreement covering about 400 tariff lines of goods, reported in mid-August 2026. (Photo: Paul Harrison, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
