World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: ACT's neurodiverse community 'cautiously welcomes' autism minister
World.content:
Neurodivergent support organisations have welcomed the creation of a dedicated autism and neurodiversity portfolio in the ACT government.

After a cabinet reshuffle following the resignation of Yvette Berry, Suzanne Orr became the Minister for Disability, Autism and Neurodiversity.

The ACT is now the first jurisdiction to include neurodiversity in a ministerial portfolio, and the second to include autism, after South Australia introduced an assistant minister for autism in 2022.

Autism Spectrum Australia (ASPECT) chief executive Jacqui Borland said the position would increase the visibility of autism across the ACT government and the community.

Jacqui Borland says she would like to see the position used to improve autistic people's outcomes across education, healthcare, employment and inclusion. (Supplied: ASPECT)

"That's important because the understanding that will grow will be of the diversity of autistic experience and the barriers that people can face in everyday life," she said.

"Of course, the understanding is one thing, but then what we hope we would see would be a translation then into practical improvements that help to make life more accessible and inclusive for autistic and neurodivergent people and their families."

Ms Borland said she would like to see the position used to improve autistic people's outcomes across education, healthcare, employment and inclusion.

"We know that there are many autistic neurodivergent people working in the government in Canberra," she said.

"So support to help those across all of those departments to be more inclusive would help those autistic neurodiverse people to be successful in their jobs, and then therefore be more successful in their everyday lives."

Calls for partnership with autistic community, specialists

Neurodivergent therapist Jacqueline Gibb said she welcomed the new position but was cautious, noting she was unsure why autism and neurodiversity were separated.

"But if it leads to real-world changes for autistic people and other people with different neurodivergences, then I'm all for it," she said.

Jacqueline Gibb created Actually Autistic Canberra, a support group for autistic adults, after noticing a lack of safe spaces. (Supplied: Jacqueline Gibb)

Ms Gibb, who is autistic herself, said she would like to see the ACT government work with the community to create autistic-led spaces.

She created Actually Autistic Canberra, a support group for autistic adults, because she noticed a lack of safe spaces.

"I would love for them to have actual partnerships with autistic people, with the autistic community," Ms Gibb said.

"Also with autistic professionals like myself who work in this space, who often do very well in delivering to autistic kids and autistic adults."

She said many in Canberra's neurodivergent community felt burnt out from advocating.

"Our community is really exhausted from all this constant having to advocate for ourselves and not being listened to," she said.

"I think we've all said it all, but we're just not being listened to."

Neurodiversity strategy a top priority

Suzanne Orr says she will prioritise developing a dedicated neurodiversity strategy and implementing the Thriving Kids model. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

Ms Orr said the new portfolio aligned with the ACT government's work to progress greater disability inclusion.

"It's fair to say there is a growing focus on autism and looking at how we can better respond to autism and make an inclusive world for everybody with autism," she told 666 ABC Canberra last month.

" But autism is not the only form of neurodivergence. There's quite a bit there. "

Model released for NDIS alternative for some autistic children The federal government reveals how its NDIS alternative for some children under nine will work.

Ms Orr said one of her priorities would be developing a dedicated neurodiversity strategy, one of the government's election promises.

She said she would also be working to implement the federal government's Thriving Kids model, aiming to divert children under nine with "mild to moderate" developmental delays and autism from the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).

"Another key priority will be working with the community and across government on the roll out of Thriving Kids services and supports to ensure children aged up to eight with autism and their parents, carers and kin with low or moderate support needs have services specific to their needs," Ms Orr said in a statement.

'Underlying uncertainty' about Thriving Kids

Jacqueline Gibb says the neurodivergent community has been critical of the Thriving Kids program.

The ACT government committed to rolling out Thriving Kids from October, over the next 18 months.

Ms Gibb said the neurodivergent community had been critical of Thriving Kids, describing it as "tokenistic".

"It feels very much like control is being taken away from the community in terms of what we can do, who we can choose, who do we work with," she said.

"It just feels very poorly thought out, and it's constantly being presented as: 'This is such a great thing for you. We're doing this as a favour to autistic people. This will be better for them.'

"I don't even know how you can really engage with an argument like that, honestly, when it's just not true."

Federal Disability and NDIS Minister Mark Butler announced the Thriving Kids program in a National Press Club address in August last year. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

Ms Borland said there was an "underlying uncertainty" from parents about what Thriving Kids would mean for them.

"When families don't have information, then they imagine the worst," she said.

"In terms of [Thriving Kids'] design … it's about really making sure that families who have children with developmental delays or developmental concerns through this period of transition to Thriving Kids don't fall through the gaps, that they do receive the services.

" If they will no longer be eligible for NDIS, then we need to make sure that they are supported and that there isn't a group of families through this transition who miss out. "

Ms Orr convened two roundtables with service providers, advocates, parents and carers earlier in the year to identify gaps in the ACT's support system.

"The ACT government will continue consultation and community engagement activities as planning for and implementation of Thriving Kids progresses," she said.

Suzanne Orr says the ACT government will continue consultation and community engagement about the planning and implementation of Thriving Kids. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Ms Borland said ASPECT had been involved in the consultation process.

She said it was important Thriving Kids was designed in partnership with neurodivergent people, and support services that worked with them.

"We have talked to them about the services that we know work in terms of supporting families, in terms of supporting young children that Thriving Kids covers, in terms of supporting and providing support for the mainstream community places where those children live, work and play," Ms Borland said.

Ms Orr said the discussion around Thriving Kids had brought autism into the government's broader consciousness.

"In doing this, what we really want to do is send that signal to people that the government is focused on this area and we are committed to doing what we can to make sure that we're including people with autism neurodivergence within our community," she said.

World.title: Ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism scandal found dead
World.content:
Black academic Jason Arday, who resigned from the University of Cambridge last week amid a high-profile plagiarism storm that featured racism claims, has been found dead.

Dr Arday, 41, was found unresponsive on Friday afternoon, local time, at an address in south London, according to the Metropolitan Police Service which did not confirm the identity of the deceased person discovered.

"We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news," Cambridge University's top administrator, Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice, said in a brief statement.

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

The scandal erupted after some academics and media reports accused Dr Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest black professor in 2023, of plagiarising parts of his doctoral thesis.

The allegations have been seized on by British right-wing newspapers and commentators who claim that he unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion policies.

Dr Arday announced on August 5 that he was resigning from both his university post as a professor and as a fellow of Jesus College, shortly after they announced probes into the various accusations.

In a letter posted online, Dr Arday had said that quitting was "the only way" to end a "difficult period", but insisted the decision should not be "mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

The police statement said officers had been called by the London Ambulance Service "following a report that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property" in the city's Battersea neighbourhood.

"Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene," it added, noting his next-of-kin had been informed.

"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

"The case is being investigated by officers from the Met's Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner."

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked [and] saddened" by the news.

She urged people to give his family "privacy through this incredibly difficult period [and] to remember there are real people with loved ones involved".

The furore around Dr Arday grew after Nathan Cofnas, a US academic and self-defined "race realist" whose Cambridge research affiliation ended in 2024 amid racism accusations, published claims about him in July.

The allegations included that multiple sections of Dr Arday's doctoral dissertation were copied from other works.

The Times and Telegraph newspapers have published several investigative articles into Dr Arday's academic work and personal life.

Some of his claims about his personal life, including that he once ran 30 marathons in 35 days and raised millions for charities, were also disputed.

In an interview with The Times earlier this month, Dr Arday admitted making academic "mistakes" but said he was being wrongly "portrayed to be a liar and a fantasist and an academic fraud".

He also alleged the "campaign to unseat me from my position" was "racially motivated".

The controversy around Dr Arday appears to have divided the Cambridge campus and wider academia.

Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism furore quits Professor Jason Arday resigned from his posts shortly after the British institution announced a probe into the various accusations against him.

A group of university academics last week wrote to Ms Prentice slamming Dr Arday's appointment and asking her to appoint an independent body to probe what happened.

Others have written joint letters in support of him.

On Wednesday, Ms Prentice had called his alleged wrongdoing "an aberration" and vowed a thorough and transparent investigation while insisting it should not be used "to cast aspersions" on other academics from ethnic minority backgrounds.

The American psychologist promised the probe would look into the "circumstances" of Dr Arday's appointment and his time in the post that would include academics from "beyond Cambridge".

Dr Arday's memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, had been published in the United States the previous day ahead of its planned release in Britain later this month. It has also attracted scrutiny.

AFP

World.title: Bezos consortium enters 'definitive agreement' to buy Liverpool stake
World.content:
A consortium containing Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is buying a minority stake in Premier League club Liverpool, the English soccer giant says.

Club owner Fenway Sports Group (FSG) said in a statement it entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale to 1892 Holdings.

The investor group is led by Amit Bhatia, who is married to a daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, and has taken a stake of more than 30 per cent in the 20-time English champion. The deal reportedly values Liverpool at around $US6 billion ($8.4 billion).

Boston-based FSG paid $US400 million to take over Liverpool in 2010 and also owns the Boston Red Sox. FSG said in July that it had been approached by the Bhatia-led consortium regarding a "strategic minority investment" in the club.

Eduardo Saverin is part of the investment group with Jeff Bezos. (Getty Images: Sam Barnes/Sportsfile)

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said in the statement.

It marks the first foray into soccer by Bezos, who, according to Forbes, is the fourth-richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US280 billion. He founded Amazon in 1994 and has been executive chairman since 2021.

Saverin is a Brazilian businessman worth about $US36 billion, according to Forbes.

Bhatia, a British-Indian entrepreneur, was the co-owner of second-tier English team Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before stepping down recently.

Amit Bhatia during his time as the chairman of Queens Park Rangers. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

"We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come," Bhatia said in the statement.

Under the leadership of FSG and its principal owner John Henry, Liverpool ended a 30-year wait to be English champion in 2020 and added another Premier League title last year. That tied Manchester United on 20 English top-flight league championships.

The club was European champion for a sixth time — a record for an English team — in 2019.

The Premier League is one of the biggest competitions in sports, with its teams now largely owned by oil-rich Gulf states or private equity.

Liverpool sack manager Arne Slot after underwhelming season The Dutchman won the Premier League title in his first season, but failed to live up to expectations the following year as Liverpool finished fifth.

Liverpool now has three of the richest people in the world as minority owners.

That does not mean, however, that the club can simply start spending recklessly in the transfer market on new players.

That is because the Premier League has financial rules in place to protect the competitive balance of the competition and ensure the financial sustainability of clubs.

In broad terms, a club's on-pitch spending is related to 85 per cent of its "football-related revenue and net profit/loss from player sales," the Premier League says.

Instead, the difference will come in how Liverpool — already one of the top teams in world soccer — is marketed more around the world under Bezos and Saverin, especially.

The deal is likely to bring more commercial revenue into the club, thereby improving its profits.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Community remembers those lost in one of Australia's worst mining disasters
World.content:
By a quiet road, near an abandoned mine in Victoria's central highlands is a new sign detailing one of Australia's worst mining disasters.

It tells the tale of 22 men who lost their lives in the pursuit of gold 140 years ago while working at The New Australasian No.2 Mine near Creswick.

The sign, installed by the Creswick Connect community group, will ensure these 22 souls will never be forgotten and serve as a reminder of the human cost behind Victoria's gold rush.

New interpretive signage aims to preserve the stories of the disaster for future generations. (ABC News: Ava Ross)

Deep personal connection

Mining historian and guide Darren Bellingham has a deep personal connection to the No.2 Mine.

On the evening of December 11, 1882, Darren's great-great-grandfather Jabez Bellingham and great-great-uncle Benjamin Bellingham began their usual night shift working in the mine.

Darren Bellingham's great-great-grandfather Jabez Bellingham. (Supplied: Darren Bellingham)

Around 5.30am the following day, they were about to knock-off when disaster struck.

Miners were digging near an abandoned shaft that had previously flooded after it was thought all the gold had been exhausted.

While they were working, a geological disturbance caused water to surge into the mine, blocking the way out and trapping 29 men almost a kilometre from the entrance.

With the clock ticking and the water rising, the group decided the men with more children were allowed to go up ladders so they could keep out of the water for longer.

The New Australasian No.2 Mine near Creswick. (Supplied: Mitchell Library)

A small number of miners managed to escape, particularly the fitter men and the stronger swimmers.

Jabez was among them, but he turned back to try and save his brother Benjamin.

The miners had found a small pocket of air, huddling together in complete darkness, about 90 metres below the surface, with only their heads above the rising water.

To keep hope alive, Jabez used his skills as the church organist and choir master to lead the men in singing, and the men prayed and sang hymns as the water rose.

Knowing rescue might never come, some scratched their final messages onto metal buckets, hoping their words would survive even if they did not.

Twenty-seven miners remained trapped underground for three days, some in the water, while huddled on timber and ladders, in a chamber roughly the size of a shipping container.

As time passed, many succumbed to exhaustion, dehydration and lack of oxygen, leaving just five survivors when rescuers finally reached them after much of the water had been pumped out.

The story of the 27 trapped miners has been preserved on signage constructed by Creswick Connect. (Supplied: James Freemantle, Creswick Connect)

The Bellingham brothers tied themselves together, fearing they might be separated if the water claimed them.

Neither man survived.

Four thousand people marched in a funeral procession for the dead miners, with 15,000 mourners watching on.

Jabez's choir sang over his grave, while Benjamin, a member of the local military corps, was honoured with a gun salute at his funeral.

An underground mine tour at Sovereign Hill offers visitors an insight into the dangerous working conditions miners had to face. (ABC News: Ava Ross)

Path to compensation

Darren Bellingham said the effects of the disaster were felt deeply across the community.

"It had a really big impact — every mine for 100 kilometres around Creswick was closed that day," Darren said.

Darren Bellingham has a deep family connection to the New Australasian No.2 Mine disaster. (ABC News: Ava Ross)

The gravity of the disaster started to make people think about compensation issues, and lack of protection for miners' families, ultimately leading to the creation of the Mining Accident Relief Fund Act two years later, which established formal compensation for victims of mining accidents.

For Darren, one detail has always stayed with his family.

"Benjamin wasn't supposed to work that day," he said.

"He took someone else's shift because he was looking for extra work, and so, he was killed and he shouldn't have been."

The memorial remembers the miners who died. (Supplied: James Freemantle, Creswick Connect)

A legacy of sacrifice

More than 140 years after one of Victoria's worst mining disasters, new interpretive signage at the site of the New Australasian No.2 Mine in Creswick aims to ensure the lives of the 22 men who died are never forgotten.

The project has been years in the making and will be officially unveiled by Creswick Connect on August 30.

Project manager James Freemantle said he hoped visitors leave with a greater appreciation and respect for the miners that helped shape what Victoria is today.

"It's so important not to forget that so many people were sacrificed," Mr Freemantle said.

"We want people to be touched by the story and to respect the lives that were lost but also think about what we ask people to do in the name of progress.

"What sacrifices do we ask people to make when you know we're trying to find profits?"

World.title: Luxury tower 'affordability' claim rejected in landmark court ruling
World.content:
A legal cloud is hanging over high-rises on the Gold Coast after a court ruled luxury apartments do not improve housing affordability simply because they increase housing supply.

The Queensland Court of Appeal ruled in July that the council's claim that a luxury high-rise would improve "housing choice and affordability" was not enough to justify exceeding the regulated height limit.

In a judgment summary, Justice Shane Doyle stated that apartments targeting the luxury market could not reasonably be considered as improvements to housing affordability.

"To add to the supply of apartments designed to cater to the luxury and more affluent market cannot, in my view, be reconciled with the ordinary meaning of the word 'affordability'," he wrote.

" To do so would be a distortion of the ordinary meaning of affordability. "

The court ruling has thrown the council's high-rise approvals into uncertainty, with councillors set to be briefed on its implications later this month.

Construction of new apartment buildings along Bilinga in January 2025. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Luxury gets 'affordability' exemption

Under the council's planning rules, developers can build up to 50 per cent above an area's height limit if they meet a list of criteria.

Those criteria cover issues from neighbourhood amenity and design to whether a project benefits "housing choice and affordability".

In 2023, developer Cielo Property Group applied to build an almost 34-metre-high tower at Pacific Parade in Bilinga, 10 metres above the suburb's height limit.

The development was also more than double the permitted density, with one bedroom per 14.9 square metres compared with the limit of one per 33 square metres.

The site of a proposed luxury high-rise at 90–92 Pacific Parade, Bilinga. (ABC Gold COast: Dominic Cansdale)

But the City of Gold Coast approved the luxury project, finding it satisfied the exemption criteria, including by benefiting "housing choice and affordability".

Nearby residents challenged that approval in the Planning and Environment Court but lost.

Court documents state the "very expensive apartments" would not provide affordable housing for low- to moderate-income earners, but could provide a "net community benefit to a more affluent segment of the market to meet their housing needs and choices".

But the Court of Appeal found that to be "an error in law", with its ruling "expected to have significance for other development applications".

Limited definition for affordability

The Court of Appeal noted that the council's planning scheme did not directly define "housing choice and affordability".

But it did define "affordable housing" as "appropriate to the needs of households with low to moderate incomes, if the members of the households will spend no more than 30 per cent of gross income on housing costs".

The council argued that "increased density is one way to increase affordability".

Higher-density towers are set to spread further across the Gold Coast. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

But the Court of Appeal disagreed, finding that simply increasing the number of homes in a luxury development was not enough to satisfy the requirement for "housing choice and affordability".

The Bilinga project has been sent back to the Planning and Environment Court for reconsideration.

Councillors will be briefed on the implications of the Court of Appeal’s decision on August 25.

The ABC understands a High Court appeal remains open to council.

'Much wider implications'

Retired lawyer Michael Sparksman challenged another Bilinga development in the Planning and Environment Court last year, on the basis it harmed the area's character and visual amenity.

He said the court had been "waving through any luxury development" on an incorrect understanding of "housing choice and affordability".

"You can't simply say that luxury apartments are affordable — luxury apartments are in the multi-million-dollar range," Mr Sparksman said.

He said the Court of Appeal decision would have "much wider implications", especially in the southern suburbs, where height limits had become a major community concern.

High-rise developments have been met with some resistance on the southern Gold Coast. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

"It sets the tone for this interpretation to run across all councils, certainly in Queensland but especially the Gold Coast where developers and council have run roughshod," he said.

"Some existing approvals will probably be challenged."

On Tuesday, the council's Planning and Regulation Committee delayed a 40-unit luxury high-rise in Palm Beach, pending legal advice on how the Court of Appeal's ruling could affect its approval.

Deputy Mayor and committee chair Mark Hammel said council was legally obliged to continue assessing development applications under the current planning scheme, but work was underway on a new scheme.

"This reinforces for me the importance of the work we are currently doing on the new planning scheme to deliver more certainty for the community and the most efficient and effective development outcomes for residents, the development industry and the courts," he said.

Cielo Property Group has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Sydney trains to run on schedule after wiring issue causes network chaos
World.content:
Trains will operate on schedule this morning after overhead wiring issues caused widespread delays across Sydney's network last night.

Hundreds of people were assisted off trains after overhead wires came down onto one of them yesterday evening.

Significant delays across Sydney's rail network continued into the night.

Commuters had to be assisted off the South Coast service between Redfern and Erskineville after overhead wire come down on the train. (Supplied: Sean Murphy)

Sydney Trains chief executive Matt Longland said all six lines were now open.

"I want to apologise to passengers who were impacted by delays on the rail network in Sydney on Friday night," he said.

"Teams have worked right through the night last night and all six lines through the area are now fully reopened with normal weekend services operating, but a reminder that track work is in place in Western Sydney today.

"We'll be investigating the root cause of the incident throughout the weekend."

Passengers using trains this weekend are being advised that planned track work is continuing today, with changes to parts of the T2, T4, T5, Blue Mountains and South Coast lines.

About 4:30pm yesterday, the South Coast Line service was travelling between Redfern and Erskineville, in Sydney's inner west, when the wires came down.

Sydney Trains says trains will run to normal service today. (Supplied: Sean Murphy)

Two other nearby trains came to a grinding halt.

Transport authorities isolated power to safely remove passengers.

Just before 7pm last night, some commuters were still being assisted off, but everyone had been cleared by 8pm.

Sydney major train delays Hundreds of people have been assisted off trains after overhead wires came down onto one of them on Friday evening.

Earlier, Sydney Trains' head of rail operations, Jas Tumber, said the cause of the wiring issue was unknown.

"This is a really significant disruption that's causing really wide ripple effects," he said.

Train passenger Sean Murphy said he left Redfern for Sutherland on the Kiama train about 4:30pm and that "the engine just stopped" five minutes later.

"The train just went basically dead," he said.

Mr Murphy said staff announced that a train ahead of them "had brought down powerlines" and to await further instructions.

World.title: Trump says he will soon declare Strait of Hormuz US territory
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says he will soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, escalating his rhetoric over the vital waterway that carries a significant share of global oil supplies.

"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated -- pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States," he said during a political rally at a police academy in New York state.

It was unclear how seriously Mr Trump intended the remark or whether it represented a new policy position.

He also told Fox News on Friday, local time, that the United States would hit Iran hard economically as Washington and Tehran struggle to reach a deal to end a nearly six-month conflict.

His comments came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US was going to apply measures that have "never been seen" on Iran as soon as next week.

The Strait of Hormuz remains a critical pressure point for global energy markets and oil prices have risen this week, with Brent crude approaching $US90 a barrel.

In Australia, the average price of unleaded remains above $2/litre, while the average price of diesel is nearing $2.50/litre.

At the Garden City rally, Mr Trump urged Americans to accept paying "a tiny little bit more for your gasoline" as the cost of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

"What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves … and we're really doing a great job," he said, adding he would never apologise for attacking Iran.

The comments underscore the growing political risk for Mr Trump as higher fuel prices collide with his campaign promise to lower energy costs, with Democrats already seeking to make the economic fallout from the Iran war an issue heading into the November midterm elections.

Trump downplays toll on sailors aboard USS Abraham Lincoln

Meanwhile, Mr Trump downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring a record-setting deployment of nearly nine months on the USS Abraham Lincoln, as concerns escalate about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier supporting US operations against Iran.

In a brief exchange with reporters before flying to New York, Mr Trump refuted that family members have raised concerns about the deployment's length and even said that the more than 260-day deployment was "not nearly long enough".

"That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it's being replaced with another very similar ship," he said when asked about the lengthy deployment.

The USS Abraham Lincoln carrier departed California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February. (Supplied: US Navy/Brian M Wilbur)

The Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran, and several Democratic lawmakers are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the carrier, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday said were "completely misrepresented".

Democratic congressman Jason Crow, who served three tours in Iraq and Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division and 75th Ranger Regiment before being elected, criticised Mr Trump's comments on X, saying he "does not care about our servicemembers or their families".

Extended deployments of carriers during the Iran conflict have triggered concerns about the impact on service members who are away from home for long periods as well as the increasing strain on the ship and its equipment.

While hostilities between the US and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the Navy has reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war.

Mr Hegseth said that the US military could maintain the blockage of Iranian ports "indefinitely".

Loading...

Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, last week left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, and is expected to replace the USS Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.

After reports emerged that sailors on the Lincoln were struggling with mental health concerns, the Navy said it had "not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship", though officials have declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.

A Navy official said that a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but that the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship's medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say whether it was being considered a suicide attempt.

US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has also pushed back on reports about poor conditions.

Reuters/AP

World.title: 'They're going to take our GST' sets alarm bells ringing in the west
World.content:
Alarm bells were literally ringing in Western Australian government offices after the "east coast clowns" launched their attack on the state's precious GST dollars.

"While we're gone, they're going to take our GST," Treasurer Rita Saffioti joked before evacuating from a fiery press conference.

It was only partly a joke.

Journalists, politicians and staffers were forced to evacuate during the media conference. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Western Australia has relied heavily on a sweetheart deal, which replaced the formula all other states rely on, to fund its economy in recent years with an extra $22 billion from the Commonwealth up to mid-2025.

That extra money has seen WA post record surpluses.

WA's leaders insist that money has been more than paid back to the nation in company tax payments and the like, and that it deserves the extra billions to enable the country's prosperity.

The Productivity Commission yesterday revealed it agreed with every other state and territory, saying the deal had produced "perverse outcomes" and created a two-tier system.

WA Premier Roger Cook came out swinging, dubbing those conclusions and the proposed fixes "dodgy, deceitful and quite frankly dumb".

That the normally mild-mannered premier was so fired up can be explained by the $6 billion hit the mining state could be up for if the deal was done away with entirely. Not that that is being suggested.

Roger Cook says WA plays a vital role in the country's economy because of its unmatched resources sector. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

How much, if any, is lost depends on the commission's final recommendations later this year and whether the federal government adopts them.

It's why WA has given up trying to convince the other states of the deal's merits, whose premiers Cook today branded as "whingers", to focus on the only two people who matter: the prime minister and his treasurer.

Loading...

Next steps a matter of politics

It was politics which got the federation into this mess, and it will almost certainly be politics which decides what happens next.

The 2018 deal was struck between then-WA premier Mark McGowan and then-prime minister Scott Morrison to resolve a political headache for the new West Australian government.

The deal was struck in 2018 between Mark McGowan (left) and Scott Morrison. (ABC News: James Carmody)

A falling iron ore price, and therefore reduced royalties flowing into the state's coffers, coincided with its GST payments falling.

WA premier lashes 'east-coast clowns' An angry Roger Cook has lashed who he calls 'east-coast clowns' over an explosive proposed shake-up of the GST carve-up.

That's because the way the GST had been carved up was about putting all states on an equal footing by offering more money to those which earned less themselves, or had higher expenses, averaged out over three years to smooth things out.

That averaging meant WA's share was falling, from the previously strong years, just as its royalties dried up.

This chart shows what happened in the years since. Not only have royalties been up because of high iron ore prices, but so too have GST payments, thanks to the deal.

The current fight is really two separate debates: should WA get extra money from the Commonwealth to help fund its mining industry, and if so, how should it get it?

For the deal's chief critic, independent economist Saul Eslake, the first answer is no.

In his view, WA isn't holding up the national economy.

"Yes, Western Australia generates a lot of exports from minerals, largely thanks to China's thirst for them and its willingness to pay hitherto unimaginable prices for them," he said.

" That's not the result of any far-sighted policies by the current or previous Western Australian governments. It's good fortune. "

Aaron Morey says running WA's economy takes an incredible amount of resources from government. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

It's an idea angrily rejected by the state, which argues the only reason WA benefits from China's hunger for iron ore is because of support offered by successive governments.

"The Productivity Commission thinks that running a world-class mining sector is as easy as ordering a cafe latte on Collins Street," Chamber of Minerals and Energy boss Aaron Morey said.

"Well, I've got news for them. It ain't."

How could this be resolved?

Despite WA's complaints, the Productivity Commission isn't necessarily arguing the state shouldn't receive extra money.

Its concern is that the GST was not designed fund particular projects or government priorities, but to even out states' fiscal capacities.

Iron ore royalties and WA's GST payments are on the up. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

That's not what is happening now.

Under the current system, WA is funded to 113 per cent of its needs, according to the commission.

The commission said any move away from fully equalising states' finances could be "proposed and defended" but needed to be clearly justified and deliver benefits.

Eslake, and others, don't believe that case has been made.

The commission would rather the GST formula is adjusted, or funding is provided another way.

The latter leaves those funds open to change at the whim of the federal government.

The former is too complex, according to the WA treasurer.

"Trying to unpick this deal will disadvantage WA," Rita Saffioti told the ABC.

The fiery press conference continued outdoors. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

She also pointed out the 2018 deal is enshrined in legislation, meaning even if Labor wanted to change it the Greens or Liberals would need to agree.

Two of WA's top federal Liberals, Michaelia Cash and Andrew Hastie, said that wouldn't happen.

"Over our dead bodies will they take a cent from Western Australia," Senator Cash said.

Mr Cook said he's spoken to the PM who told him "arrangements in place for Western Australia will remain".

Basil Zempilas isn't counting on the prime minister to save the day in WA. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Anthony Albanese, who backtracked on negative gearing, who backtracked on capital gains tax," state opposition leader Basil Zempilas said.

"How can any West Australian trust that he is not going to backtrack on what is right for West Australians when it comes to our share of the GST?"

Over to Albanese

That's one way of seeing those broken promises.

The other is that Labor might think twice about opening up another fight.

Especially when that fight would risk the WA seats which put it into power in 2022 and kept it there in 2025, at the same time as One Nation threatens to up-end the political landscape.

It's also possible the Commonwealth could try to find a way of undoing the current deal without WA losing out, at least too much.

If it all goes pear shaped though, Western Australia always has the nuclear option up its sleeve.

Anthony Albanese famously writes and signs 'No Change To WA GST' on the forearm of a journalist in 2019. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

"Is succession tempting?" a journalist asked yesterday.

"Every Western Australian premier has that thought from time to time," Cook said.

"But it's not an option. We don't want to be separate from the rest of Australia.

"We just sincerely believe that we should not be penalised for doing the heavy lifting on economic activity."

World.title: Former Cambridge professor Jason Arday, who resigned amid plagiarism row, found dead
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeTragedy Former Cambridge professor Jason Arday, who resigned amid plagiarism row, found dead August 15, 2026 — 7:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Jason Arday, a former University of Cambridge professor who was at the centre of a plagiarism scandal, has been found dead, British media reported on Friday. Arday, who was 37 when he became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, resigned after he came under intense media pressure, with weeks of allegations about plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments. Jason Arday was Cambridge University’s youngest black professor. Joe Giddens/PA via AP The Times and Telegraph newspapers, along with the BBC and Sky News, reported that Arday, 41, was found “unresponsive” inside a home in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon (London time). In a statement issued by his publisher Simon & Schuster UK, Arday’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.



“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone,” the family said, adding that for three years Arday was “subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse ... by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him”. Related Article University Star scholar resigns from Cambridge amid plagiarism row Cambridge vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university would investigate the circumstances around Arday’s employment, said she was “desperately saddened” by the news. “Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time,” she said. In resigning as professor of sociology of education, Arday wrote in a statement that “the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.



He said his stepping down should not “be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me”. He has denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate. Supporters, including more than two dozen academics and politicians, had described the plagiarism allegations as a “smear campaign” designed to undermine Arday and other black people who hold “positions of influence”. Arday’s appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens. Police said: “At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636.

World.title: From playboy to bankrupt. The $1.8b rise and fall of Jon Adgemis
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesPubs From playboy to bankrupt. The $1.8b rise and fall of Jon Adgemis Kishor Napier-Raman August 15, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aspiring pub baron Jon Adgemis once lived a gilt-plated life. The former KPMG rainmaker (he made partner aged 28) cruised Sydney’s eastern suburbs in a black Maserati, entertained associates on a luxury Italian vintage yacht, arrived at the Melbourne Cup by helicopter, and paraded a series of glamorous Birkin-toting girlfriends at society events. Jon Adgemis has been in the sights of the ATO, which raided his offices in 2024, for at least two years. Dominic Lorrimer Then the good times came crashing down. The Australian Taxation Office began circling his debt-fuelled businesses, before eventually forcing them into bankruptcy last October owing $1.8 billion. This week, liquidators from BRI Ferrier spent days picking through the wreckage at a Federal Court examination, and the details weren’t pretty. The yacht, Hiilani, has been sold to pay Adgemis’ debts. So have most of the cars. Model Cheyenne Tozzi, who split from Adgemis in 2017, has been asked to give evidence at the examination, which this week has finally shed some light on the billion-dollar mystery of how Adgemis’ Public Hospitality Group collapsed.



After leaving KPMG, Adgemis set his sights on building an entertainment empire to rival that of another perma-tanned eastern suburbs playboy, Merivale’s Justin Hemmes. He made a bet on Australia’s post-pandemic appetite for pleasure, buying up 22 entertainment venues in Sydney and Melbourne. Crucially, he made the bet using others’ money, fuelling his purchases with cheap debt from investors wooed by unrealistic valuations. Jon Adgemis had owned the private yacht Hiilani, which once belonged to Hollywood star Shirley Temple. The finer details of how Public Hospitality collapsed are particularly damning. In documents supplied to the court, the ATO said it was examining about $1 billion in spending incurred by one of Adgemis’ companies, alleging that it had received $77 million in GST refunds as part of a sham tax arrangement. Alexander Andruska, a Woollahra councillor and a long-term Adgemis lieutenant said that those refunds were essential to running the business. He alleged that his former boss had used that money to fund his exorbitant lifestyle.



“It was very stressful. I wanted to bloody blow my brains out,” Andruska said of trying to manage Adgemis’ finances. Related Article Pubs ‘One disaster after another’: Failed pub baron’s former accountant turns on him Accountant Sam Stringer, who was engaged by Adgemis after an audit by the ATO, told the court that the companies were not in a good financial position, and that trying to lodge their tax returns was a “mammoth” task. “We were given very little information. They were extremely disorganised and impossible to get information from,” he said. On Monday, Damien Hodgkinson, a co-founder of teal independent bank-roller Climate200 and an associate of Adgemis’ since their time as KPMG partners, was in court. The court heard that the pair had conspired to install Adgemis’ friend Marco Bettelli as sole director of Linchpin, a supposedly separate company that began operating some Public Hospitality Group venues amid financial troubles last year.



While several of Adgemis’ associates were grilled by the liquidator’s barrister Michael Rose, the man at the centre was conspicuously absent. Adgemis spent just seconds in the witness box, before his lawyers moved a motion to have the matter set aside as an abuse of process and to have the liquidators’ solicitors, ERA Legal, barred from acting. If Adgemis’ examination proceeds, his lawyers want it conducted in secret, away from the prying eyes of the media, a move that is being challenged by news organisations including this masthead. His sister, Despina Adgemis, took a similar approach, failing to appear on Thursday when scheduled. Her lawyers, Hamilton Locke, said she had never received a summons. Rose, counsel for the liquidators’, said that she had, whereupon her lawyers produced a medical certificate saying she was unable to attend. Despina is married to Rodd Boland, another KPMG man whom Andruska alleged was made a “straw director” by Adgemis of several companies last year. Boland and Adgemis previously lived at a Rose Bay property owned by Jon and their mother Rose, which was seized by lenders last year. While Adgemis’ family appears to be sticking by him, former friends are jumping ship. Andruska, who has worked with Adgemis since 2012, tried to downplay their friendship. “I do have a soft spot in my heart for Jon, but at the same time, he has caused me over a decade of stress, heartbreak and financial ruin,” Andruska told this masthead. “It’s a very toxic relationship.”





Madsen is currently being sued in a bankruptcy judgment by HG Capital, which invests on behalf of wealthy Vietnamese Sydneysiders, over the millions lent to a collapsed company that he and Adgemis were directors of. Preliminary hearings in that matter, to which Adgemis is also a party, were also underway this week in the NSW Supreme Court, just downstairs from where the Adgemis examinations took place. All that’s left now of Adgemis’ businesses is a mountain of debt, a conga-line of cranky creditors, and hefty legal bills. Adgemis is understood to be footing his own legal bills, and is currently working as a consultant for a number of clients. He is represented by solicitor Jamie DiMeo and barrister Miles Condon, SC, who reportedly command fees of $15,000 a day. On Wednesday, high-profile criminal lawyer Bryan Wrench, who is busy acting for Alan Jones in his indecent assault trial and lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood, who is facing the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s probe into a Liberal Party sub-faction, made a cameo in court. Wrench and Adgemis have had a relationship for some time: the solicitor most recently represented the businessman during ASIC’s prosecution of Cameron in 2021, and more recently when he pleaded guilty to a low-range drink-driving charge in 2024. And what of the pubs at the heart of his empire? Most are being sold off or restructured. Some never opened, and those that did hardly set the dining scene alight. Controversial celebrity chef George Calombaris was made Public Hospitality Group’s culinary director, later joining Hodgkinson’s Linchpin, where he started serving up “Aussie, old-school, Chinese food” out of the Empire Hotel in Annandale. Good Food delivered Calombaris’ efforts at Double Happy a scathing 11.5 out of 20. “One night, there’s a cluster of dead flies floating in the soy sauce on our table,” national restaurant editor Callan Boys wrote. World.title: Luigi Mangione admits killing insurance CEO, asks to void state murder trial
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCrime Luigi Mangione admits killing insurance CEO, asks to void state murder trial Michael Koziol Updated August 15, 2026 — 5:55am ,first published 2:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Luigi Mangione admitted to fatally shooting health insurance chief executive Brian Thompson, pleading guilty to federal charges and immediately filing to have his state murder trial voided under double jeopardy provisions. The 28-year-old told a federal courtroom in New York on Friday (US time): “On the morning of December 4, 2024, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan, and he died.” A courtroom sketch depicts Luigi Mangione sitting between his attorneys on Friday. AP He pleaded guilty to stalking the insurance executive resulting in death – serious charges that could result in a lifetime prison sentence, as US District Judge Margaret Garnett reminded him on Friday. The brazen crime, early in the morning on a midtown Manhattan street, shocked the world. It also generated sympathy for Mangione from parts of the community amid broader controversy over access to healthcare in America. For some people, he became something of a pin-up or political prisoner.



In court, Mangione said he researched details of UnitedHealthcare’s annual investor conference in December 2024 after suffering a broken back and navigating the health insurance system. He said he then used a 3-D printer to make part of a gun and travelled to New York with the intent of killing Thompson. There was no plea agreement, and federal prosecutors noted they were free to seek the maximum penalty under the law. Mangione’s lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said she immediately filed to have the state charges dismissed. Bloomberg Later, outside court, Mangione’s lawyer Karen Friedman Agnifilo told reporters she had immediately filed to have Mangione’s state charges – including second degree murder – voided under double jeopardy laws. “Mr Mangione has accepted full responsibility for the death of Brian Thompson,” she said. “He endured years of severe debilitating pain … He believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life.”



Agnifilo said her client had been unfairly treated since the outset, noting he successfully fought off terrorism charges and other federal charges that carried the death penalty. “It was a single tragic event, yet he is being prosecuted twice for the same conduct … New York law does not allow a person to be prosecuted and punished twice for the exact same crime.” Mangione at a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan Criminal Court in New York on August 11. Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post via AP New York district attorney Alvin Bragg is set to oppose Mangione’s attempt to void the state trial. Jury selection is due to begin on September 8, though it will likely be delayed. Garnett set sentencing on the federal charges for December 18. It was widely expected Mangione would plead guilty to the federal charges and attempt to have the state trial voided after prosecutors and the defence scheduled Friday’s unplanned hearing.



Thompson’s widow sat in the front row of the gallery with other members of his family, and there was a large media presence inside and outside court. Federal US attorney Jamie McDonald, whose office led the federal case against Mangione, told a news conference that there could be no justification for the actions the 28-year-old had admitted. US attorney Jamie McDonald said “there can be no celebrity in assassination”. Bloomberg Mangione prepared carefully, tracked Thompson’s whereabouts, conducted surveillance and used a silencer, McDonald said. After shooting twice at close range, he ran away and left his victim to die. “This was not a spontaneous act of violence. It was deliberate, calculated and premeditated,” McDonald said.



“The defendant committed this murder in an attempt to draw public attention to his dislike of certain businesses. But we live in a civilised society governed by the rule of law. We debate, we disagree, we protest. We do not commit murder. Related Article Crime Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial? “No grievance, political belief or ideological cause can ever justify murder. There can be no celebrity in assassination. Any person who celebrates, encourages, or excuses actions like these is fundamentally wrong.” Mangione had previously pleaded not guilty to the federal charges, which at the time included murder and weapons offences carrying the death penalty. Those two were later dropped. Experts say it is legally complex whether Mangione will be able to escape a state murder trial. The key legal question is whether the offences are considered distinct enough to mean that double jeopardy provisions do not apply.



A man holds a sign outside Manhattan’s Federal Court. Inside, Mangione admitted to killing health insurance executive Brian Thompson. AP Photo/Ryan Murphy “It’s actually a pretty interesting legal question,” former New York prosecutor Berit Berger told this masthead ahead of Friday’s hearing. “New York’s a little different than other states. My guess is this will not preclude the New York case from going forward, but it’s a little bit more complicated.” New York has stronger protections for the defendant not to face dual proceedings than many states, Berger said. In most cases, these circumstances would at least delay the state trial, but the court would be under pressure not to delay it too long given the public interest, she said. World.title: The most underrated film of the 21st century? It’s nice, guys
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict The most underrated film of the 21st century? It’s nice, guys In this column, we deliver hot (and cold) takes on pop culture, judging whether a subject is overrated or underrated. Tom W. Clarke August 15, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The best film of 2016 was a stylish homage to old school Hollywood and a Los Angeles lost to time. A love letter to a type of movie they don’t make any more, brought to life with a brilliant original soundtrack, rapid-fire dialogue, and a star-studded cast led by Ryan Gosling. No, not La La Land. Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe in The Nice Guys, a guaranteed fun time. Sydney Morning Herald It’s The Nice Guys, the criminally under-seen neo-noir comedy, starring Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe. Unlike La La Land, it absolutely bombed at the box office, and unlike La La Land, it didn’t almost win best picture at the Oscars. However, it’s well overdue for a re-evaluation: this is the best cinematic comedy of the past 15 years, and the most underrated film of the 21st century. It has everything you could ever want in a movie: comedy, drama, action, mystery, amazing stunts, fun outfits, outlandish twists, endlessly quotable dialogue, and two of the most acclaimed male movie stars operating at the absolute height of their powers.



The Nice Guys is a story of private eye Holland March (Ryan Gosling) and enforcer-for-hire Jackson Healy (Russell Crowe) who reluctantly team up to investigate the disappearance of a young woman, Amelia (Margaret Qualley), getting hilariously lost in the seedy underbelly beneath the glamour of 1970s Los Angeles, and unwittingly stumbling into a massive web of conspiracy and corruption. Angourie Rice, then just 13 when she started filming, holds her own against Gosling and Crowe. As the writer of the Lethal Weapon films and Last Action Hero, and director of Kiss Kiss Bang Bang and Iron Man 3, Shane Black had established a reputation for tight, exciting scripts and upending the expectations of action movies. The Nice Guys is his masterpiece, taking the Shane Black experience to the mountaintop and riding a flaming dinner tray straight down it. The script crackles with the kind of dialogue that leaves you breathless, both from laughter and sheer pace. The labyrinthine mystery box plot is twisty enough for you to get lost in, without ever feeling stupider than our loveable protagonists. Gosling flexes his comic chops years before his himbo Ken, while Crowe is pure charisma as the gruff straight man. AP



And Black recreates old school LA as well as, if not better than, Tarantino’s Oscar-winning Once Upon a Time in Hollywood would a few years later. As our hapless investigators fumble their way around town, we are treated to a vivid dreamscape of the glitz and glamour of Hollywood’s elite, as well as its dirty, desperate backstages. The supporting cast is outstanding. Australia’s Angourie Rice has her breakout as the precocious Holly, more than holding her own against Hollywood heavyweights. Qualley stuns in just her second film, and the ever-enjoyable Matt Bomer shows up as a vicious assassin with an unfortunate haircut. Ultimately though, the film is elevated into true classic territory by the unlikely chemistry between Gosling and Crowe. The mystery is fun, the big set pieces are impressive, but it all takes a back seat to the sheer delight that is watching the two actors bicker like an old married couple as they fall through fences, crash cars, and barely avoid being murdered by assassins. Their dynamic is pure gold, in the vein of other unlikely buddy action-comedies like 1982’s 48 Hrs and 1988’s Midnight Run. Gosling, in a bad tie and glorious moustache, a cigarette dangling loosely from his lips like a part of his body he’s never used before, is so accident-prone and easily overwhelmed it’s hard to imagine a worse job for him than private investigator. Crowe, the straight man, a cynical bruiser whose heart is slowly cracked open, is a man who lets his fists do the talking out of preference rather than lack of intelligence.



Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Eight-episode seasons are ruining TV. Bring back the 22-episode binge Gyan Yankovich Lifestyle Editor Gosling finds the outer edges of his remarkable comedic chops, going for broke in every scene, throwing himself into prat falls and cartoonish sobs, and giving the first glimpse of the empty-headed himbo that would become his iconic role as Ken in Barbie. Bouncing off Gosling’s frantic, trembling energy is Crowe in the best performance of his career. As opposed to his award-winning and Very Serious turns in Gladiator and A Beautiful Mind, here his natural charisma shines through and he finds more layers than any of his previous Oscar bait ever did. Had it found a larger audience, it might be just as oft-quoted as the likes of Anchorman, Superbad and Step Brothers. Perhaps The Nice Guys is destined for a slower revelation, a cult hit that finds its audience years later, a la Office Space. Either way, it’s a guaranteed good time.
